provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of the Dhammapada, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (F. Max Müller 1881; Albert J. Edmunds 1902) and checked against the Pali; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, chapter by chapter.
sourcesCited: Pali, the original text of the Dhammapada
F. Max Müller, The Dhammapada (1881, Sacred Books of the East, public domain)
Albert J. Edmunds, Hymns of the Faith (1902, public domain)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders the Dhammapada in plain modern English that keeps the proverbial weight and memorable shape of the Buddha's verses — the mind that makes the world, the craving that makes the suffering, and the path that leads beyond — while shedding the Victorian diction of the older translations.
introduction: The Dhammapada is a collection of some four hundred short verses — sayings of the Buddha gathered by theme: the twin verses, earnestness, the mind, the fool, the wise, anger, craving, the path. It is the most loved and most quoted book in Buddhism, meant to be learned by heart and turned over a line at a time. Read it slowly; each verse is a whole teaching.

divergences.phrase: All that we are is shaped by what we have thought; the mind goes before everything
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's famous opening cadence but restore the literal force of the Pali manopubbangama ("mind goes first / mind precedes"), making explicit that the mind leads, makes, and composes all things rather than only that we are a "result."
divergences.note: The Pali manopubbangama dhamma manomaya literally says the mind goes before the dhammas and they are mind-made. Müller's beloved "all that we are is the result of what we have thought" is interpretive; we preserve its music while adding the active sense that the mind goes before and makes everything.

divergences.phrase: Hatred ends only by love—this is the ancient and unchanging law
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali sanantano dhammo as "the ancient and unchanging law" rather than merely "an old rule," and place "Hatred is never ended by hatred" first as a freestanding proverb.
divergences.note: Sanantana means perennial, timeless, eternal—a law that has always held, not just a custom of long standing. "Old rule" understates it; "ancient and unchanging law" keeps the weight without softening the meaning.

divergences.phrase: a corrupted mind / craving breaks through an undisciplined mind
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "an evil thought" (v.1) and "passion will break through an unreflecting mind" (v.13).
divergences.lectio: We render padutthena manasa as "a corrupted mind" and raga as "craving" rather than the vaguer Victorian "passion," and translate the Pali sense of an untrained, undisciplined (abhavita) mind directly.
divergences.note: Müller's "passion" blurs raga, which is desire/craving/lust in the technical Buddhist sense; "craving" links it to the book's central theme. "Unreflecting" understates abhavita, "undeveloped/untrained"; "undisciplined" keeps the image of the leaky roof exact.

divergences.phrase: the path of immortality (Nirvana) … the path of death
divergences.older: Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death (Müller, 1881)
divergences.lectio: Heedfulness is the path to the deathless; heedlessness is the path to death.
divergences.note: The Pali reads appamado amatapadam, pamado maccuno padam. Amata is literally 'the deathless' — the standard epithet for Nibbana — so we keep that vivid image rather than the abstract 'immortality,' and let 'Nirvana' speak for itself in the verses where the Pali names it (23, 32).

divergences.phrase: earnestness / thoughtlessness
divergences.older: earnestness … thoughtlessness (Müller, 1881)
divergences.lectio: heedfulness … heedlessness / carelessness
divergences.note: This whole chapter turns on the single Pali word appamada (and its opposite pamada), a key term that recurs across the book. It means vigilance, diligence, an unbroken wakefulness of mind — not Müller's Victorian 'earnestness,' which sounds like mere sincerity. We render it 'heedfulness' consistently so the reader can track the term.

divergences.phrase: like a racer, leaving behind the hack
divergences.older: the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack (Müller, 1881)
divergences.lectio: the wise leave them far behind, like a swift horse leaving a slow one in its dust
divergences.note: The Pali image (abalassam va sighasso) is a fast horse outrunning a weak or worn-out one. 'Hack' is now obscure slang for a tired nag, so we make the picture plain — swift horse against slow — while keeping the racing energy of the line.

divergences.phrase: his trembling and unsteady thought
divergences.older: a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought (Müller 1881)
divergences.lectio: the wise straighten the mind — restless and unsteady
divergences.note: Müller renders Pali citta as 'thought' throughout this chapter, but citta is the mind/heart as a whole — the seat of intention and feeling, not a single passing thought. The Lectio edition reads it as 'the mind' consistently, so the chapter's argument (the untamed mind versus the tamed) holds together; the arrow-maker simile is kept intact.

divergences.phrase: rushing wherever it listeth
divergences.older: flighty, rushing wherever it listeth (Müller 1881)
divergences.lectio: light and quick, settling wherever it pleases
divergences.note: The Pali yatthakāmanipātinaṃ means 'alighting wherever it wishes' — the image is a bird or insect lighting where it likes, not headlong rushing. 'Listeth' is archaic for 'wishes/pleases'; Lectio keeps the sense of willful, restless landing while dropping the Victorian verb.

divergences.phrase: a wrongly-directed mind will do us greater mischief
divergences.older: a wrongly-directed mind will do us greater mischief … a well-directed mind will do us greater service (Müller 1881)
divergences.lectio: a misdirected mind will do you far worse … far greater is its gift
divergences.note: The chapter's culminating image, and the reason citta must be read as 'mind': a mind aimed wrong (micchāpaṇihitaṃ) harms you more than any enemy, while a mind aimed right (sammāpaṇihitaṃ) helps you more than any parent. 'Mischief/service' undersells the stakes; Lectio sharpens the contrast to 'far worse' and 'greater gift' without adding anything not in the Pali.

divergences.phrase: As the bee takes the nectar and flies off without harming the flower, its color, or its scent
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's image exactly but free its diction: "takes the nectar and flies off" for "collects nectar and departs," and "without harming the flower, its color, or its scent."
divergences.note: The Pali (yathāpi bhamaro pupphaṃ vaṇṇagandhaṃ aheṭhayaṃ) says the bee leaves the flower's color and scent unhurt — the picture of the monk who takes only his alms-food from the village and damages nothing. The image is the whole point of the verse, so we preserve it intact and only modernize the verbs.

divergences.phrase: full of color but with no scent … the fine words of one who speaks well but does not act
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly."
divergences.lectio: We render subhāsitā (well-spoken) as "fine words" and akubbato (not doing) as "does not act," and let the contrast of the two verses carry the point — color without scent is fine words that bear no fruit; color with scent is fine words that bear fruit.
divergences.note: The crux is that the flower's beauty (color) is the speech, and its scent is the action that makes the speech bear fruit. Müller's "fruitless words" is interpretive; we hold the flower-image steady across both verses (color, scent) and let "does not act" / "acts on them, and they bear fruit" supply the meaning the Pali draws from the same picture.

divergences.phrase: the fragrance of the good travels even against the wind
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the odour of good people travels even against the wind; a good man pervades every place."
divergences.lectio: We render satañ ca gandho as "the fragrance of the good" rather than "the odour of good people," and sabbā disā sappuriso pavāti as "a good person reaches every quarter."
divergences.note: "Odour" now carries a faintly bad smell in modern English, the opposite of the verse's sense, so we use "fragrance" to match "the scent of flowers" earlier in the line. The famous paradox — that ordinary scent cannot go against the wind but a good person's reaches every direction — is kept exact; "reaches every quarter" preserves sabbā disā (all directions) without the Victorian "pervades."

divergences.phrase: long is the round of rebirth to the fool
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law."
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali samsaro, rendering it "the round of rebirth" rather than flattening it to "life," so the famous triple comparison—long night, long road, long samsara—lands with its full weight.
divergences.note: The Pali reads dīgho bālāna saṃsāro: literally "long is samsara to fools." Saṃsāra is the wandering-on through repeated birth and death, the cycle the teaching exists to end—not merely a single "life." Müller's "life" loses the doctrinal point that the fool's ignorance is what makes the cycle endless; "the round of rebirth" keeps it, and matches our handling of samsara elsewhere in the book.

divergences.phrase: the fool who knows he is a fool is wise at least in that
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far."
divergences.lectio: We keep the shape of this beloved paradox but plain it up—"knows he is a fool" and "wise at least in that"—so the proverb reads as cleanly aloud in modern English as it does in the Pali.
divergences.note: The Pali yo bālo maññati bālyaṃ paṇḍito vāpi tena so turns on the word-play of bāla (fool) and paṇḍita (wise). The point is that self-knowledge is itself a kind of wisdom, while the fool who imagines himself wise is the true fool. Müller's "foolishness … so far" is faithful but stiff; we preserve the antithesis and the bite without the Victorian cadence.

divergences.phrase: no more than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup."
divergences.lectio: We render the simile as "a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup" (and in 65 "the tongue tastes the flavor"), keeping the exact image while dropping Müller's "perceives," which oddly grants the spoon a faculty of perception it is precisely meant to lack.
divergences.note: The Pali dabbī sūparasaṃ yathā contrasts the spoon (dabbī), which stirs the soup its whole life and never tastes it, with the tongue (jivhā, v.65), which tastes at the first touch. The image is about contact without understanding: the fool may sit beside the wise for a lifetime and absorb nothing. "Tastes" is the natural English verb for both spoon and tongue and keeps the paired verses parallel, as the Pali does.

divergences.phrase: follow the one who shows your faults, as a guide to buried treasure
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found … follow that wise man."
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali image: the wise person is not one who shows you where treasure lies, but one who shows you your own faults, and whom you should follow as you would a guide to buried treasure.
divergences.note: The Pali nidhinam va pavattaram yam passe vajjadassinam means "one who points out faults, as one who reveals hidden treasure." Müller mistakes the grammar and makes the treasure literal; the point is that honest reproof is itself the treasure. The corrected reading (confirmed against the Pali) is the one the verse is famous for.

divergences.phrase: as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by praise or blame
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's celebrated rock simile nearly intact, but say "are not moved" for samiñjanti rather than the weaker "falter not," and put "praise or blame" in the natural English order.
divergences.note: Pali selo yatha ekaghano vatena na samirati, evam nindapasamsasu na samiñjanti pandita. Samiñjanti is "to be stirred, to waver, to be moved"; "falter" narrows it to failing nerve. "Not moved by praise or blame" keeps the rock's stillness against both winds, which is the whole force of the line.

divergences.phrase: few cross to the other shore; the rest run up and down the near bank
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore (become Arhats); the other people here run up and down the shore."
divergences.lectio: We render the contrast plainly as crossing to "the other shore" versus running "up and down the near bank," letting the river image stand on its own without the parenthetical gloss inside the verse.
divergences.note: The Pali paragami (gone to the far shore) is the standard metaphor for reaching Nirvana, set against tiramevanudhavati, running along this bank. Naming "Arhats" mid-verse, as Müller does, breaks the picture; we keep the image clear and let verse 86 ("cross beyond the reach of death") carry the meaning, as the Pali does.

divergences.phrase: no more fever of pain
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "There is no suffering for him who has finished his journey, and abandoned grief."
divergences.lectio: We restore the literal Pali pariḷāho na vijjati—"no fever"—rather than the flat "no suffering." The word names the burning of craving and grief; "fever" keeps the heat of the image.
divergences.note: The Pali pariḷāha means a burning, a fever, the heat of passion or distress. Müller's "no suffering" is true but generic; the verse's force is that the one who has finished the journey is past the fever itself—the inner burning is gone, not merely the consequence. Edmunds (1902) likewise reaches for the heat-image, and we keep it.

divergences.phrase: They store up nothing
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Men who have no riches, who live on recognised food."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali sannicayo natthi literally as "they store up nothing" rather than Müller's interpretive "have no riches." The point is the act of hoarding—of any kind—not poverty.
divergences.note: Sannicaya is accumulation, laying things by, hoarding (of food, of goods, of merit, even of future becoming). "Have no riches" narrows it to money and sounds like mere poverty; the arhat's mark is that he amasses nothing at all, taking only what the present needs. We keep "understand the food they eat for what it is" for pariññāta-bhojanā, the mindful knowing of food, rather than Müller's "recognised food."

divergences.phrase: their track cannot be followed, like the path of birds across the sky
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "their path is difficult to understand, like that of birds in the air."
divergences.lectio: We sharpen ākāse va sakuntānaṃ padaṃ to "their track cannot be followed"—a trail that leaves no mark—rather than the vaguer "difficult to understand."
divergences.note: The Pali padaṃ here is a footprint, a track, a trace; the image is that a bird in flight leaves no path behind it to follow, just as the liberated one leaves no trace in the round of becoming for craving or for others to trace. "Difficult to understand" turns a concrete image into an abstraction; "track cannot be followed" keeps the picture exact and lets the meaning carry.

divergences.phrase: the one word of sense that brings peace
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's literal contrast but render the Pali so the proverb stands on its own: a single meaningful word outweighs a thousand empty ones, and the result is peace rather than merely becoming "quiet."
divergences.note: The Pali ekam atthapadam ("one word of meaning/benefit") set against a thousand anatthapadahi ("words without meaning"); the closing yam sutva upasammati is "hearing which one is calmed/stilled"—genuine inner peace, not just falling silent. "Brings peace" keeps the spiritual weight without softening the literal sense.

divergences.phrase: the one who conquers himself is the greatest conqueror of all
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors."
divergences.lectio: We tighten the famous line to a single arc—a thousand thousand foes set against the one foe that matters, oneself—so the proverb lands with the force the Pali gives it.
divergences.note: Yo sahassam sahassena sangame manuse jine, ekam ca jeyya attanam, sa ve sangamajuttamo. The chapter's centerpiece: outward conquest, however vast, is nothing beside self-conquest. Müller's wording is accurate but diffuse; we preserve every element while restoring the punch of a battlefield proverb.

divergences.phrase: a single day lived in virtue / a single day in which you see how all things rise and pass away
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "a life of one day is better if a man is virtuous and reflecting" … "not seeing beginning and end … if a man sees beginning and end."
divergences.lectio: We render the refrain so the contrast is immediate—one true day against a hundred empty years—and translate udayabbaya as "how all things rise and pass away" rather than the opaque "beginning and end."
divergences.note: The Pali udayabbaya ("rise and fall") names the direct insight into impermanence—watching phenomena arise and dissolve—which is the heart of this stretch of verses. Müller's "beginning and end" loses the meditative meaning; "rise and pass away" restores it. Likewise amatapada (v.114) is "the deathless," Nibbana's standard epithet, kept consistent with our rendering in earlier chapters.

divergences.phrase: Drop by drop the water-pot is filled; little by little the fool fills himself with evil
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little."
divergences.lectio: We tighten the Pali image (udabindunipātena udakumbho pi pūrati) to the proverbial "Drop by drop the water-pot is filled," and let the same line stand for both verses—evil in 121, good in 122—so the paired teaching reads as the matched set it is in the Pali.
divergences.note: The verse turns on a single, famous figure: a clay pot filling unnoticed, one drop at a time. Müller's "by the falling of water-drops" is accurate but slack; the strength of the proverb is its rhythm. We keep the literal pot and drops and the "little by little" (anupubbena), changing nothing of the sense, only restoring the memorable cadence the Pali has and the Victorian phrasing loses.

divergences.phrase: A hand with no wound on it may carry poison unharmed … no evil touches the one who does no evil
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "He who has no wound on his hand, may touch poison with his hand; poison does not affect one who has no wound; nor is there evil for one who does not commit evil."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali natthi pāpaṃ akubbato as "no evil touches the one who does no evil," keeping the verb "touches" so the hand-and-poison image and its moral lesson share the same word, as the Pali's logic intends.
divergences.note: The whole verse is one extended simile: poison cannot enter an unbroken skin, and so evil cannot enter one who commits none (Pāṇimhi ce vaṇo nāssa … natthi pāpaṃ akubbato). Müller breaks the parallel by switching from "touch" to a flat "nor is there evil for one who does not commit evil." We hold the simile together—poison does not touch the unwounded hand; evil does not touch the one who does no evil—without adding anything not in the Pali.

divergences.phrase: nowhere in all the world is there a place where you can escape your own evil deed
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "is there known a spot in the whole world where death could not overcome (the mortal)."
divergences.lectio: We restore the standard Pali reading, which ends not with "death" but with pāpakammā—"an evil deed." The verse says there is no spot on earth where one may be freed from one's own evil deed (yatthaṭṭhito mucceyya pāpakammā).
divergences.note: Müller's printed text reads maccu ("death") at the close, but the received Pali of Papavagga 127 ends with pāpakammā, and the verse's own framing—and the chapter title, "Evil"—is about the inescapable fruit of a wrong deed, not death in general. The prompt's directive and the Pali agree against Müller's word here. We follow the Pali: nowhere—sky, sea, or mountain cave—can you outrun the deed you have done.

divergences.phrase: Everyone trembles at the rod
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali sabbe tasanti dandassa literally as "everyone trembles at the rod," keeping the physical danda (stick, staff, rod) that gives the whole chapter its name, rather than the abstract "punishment."
divergences.note: Danda is a real stick or rod—the cowherd's staff in verse 135, the rod laid down in 142, the weapon raised against the harmless in 137. Müller's "punishment" hides the concrete image and breaks the thread that ties the chapter together. "The rod" keeps the picture and lets the reader feel the blow each verse is about, while "others are just like yourself" makes the Pali's golden-rule reasoning (attanam upamam katva, "making oneself the measure") plain.

divergences.phrase: like a gong that is cracked and gives no sound
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "If, like a shattered metal plate (gong), thou utter not, then thou hast reached Nirvana."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's gong but free its diction—"a gong that is cracked and gives no sound" for "a shattered metal plate"—and render esa patto'si nibbanam as having "come close to Nirvana," the verse's promise to the one who answers anger with silence.
divergences.note: The Pali kamso upahato yatha is a struck bronze gong that has been flattened or cracked so that it no longer rings—dull and silent. The image is exact: the person who will not retaliate, who absorbs a harsh word and gives back no sound, has stilled the strife (sarambha) in himself and stands at the threshold of Nirvana. "Cracked and gives no sound" keeps the picture concrete where "shattered metal plate" goes vague.

divergences.phrase: Whoever takes up the rod against those who are unarmed and harmless
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "A fool does not know when he commits his evil deeds: but the wicked man burns by his own deeds, as if burnt by fire."
divergences.lectio: We follow the received Pali of verse 137—yo dandena adandesu appadutthesu dussati, "whoever does violence with the rod to those who are unarmed and harmless"—which opens the famous tenfold-punishment passage of verses 137-140. Müller's printed line is an aberrant reading that severs verse 137 from the list of ten states it is meant to introduce.
divergences.note: Müller's edition prints at 137 a line that properly belongs with verse 136 (the fool burned by his own deeds), leaving 138-140 with no head. The standard Pali, confirmed across the tradition, begins the chapter's centerpiece here: harm the harmless and you will swiftly meet one of ten miseries. We restore the Pali reading the prompt names—"the rod that falls on the harmless brings tenfold suffering"—so the passage stands whole, and keep Müller's "burned as if by fire" at its rightful place in 136.

divergences.phrase: the maker of this house … you shall not build this house again
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Looking for the maker of this tabernacle, I shall have to run through a course of many births … But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again."
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali gahakāraka as "house-builder" rather than Müller's archaic and religiously loaded "maker of this tabernacle," and render this as the Buddha's own cry of enlightenment — spoken, the tradition holds, at the foot of the Bodhi tree — keeping its full weight: "House-builder, now you are seen! You shall not build this house again."
divergences.note: The Pali gahakāraka (anekajāti saṃsāraṃ sandhāvissaṃ … gahakārakaṃ gavesanto) is literally the builder of a house, the craving (taṇhā) that frames the "house" of the body birth after birth; "tabernacle" imports a Biblical word the Pali does not have. These are among the most famous lines in all Buddhism, traditionally the Buddha's first words upon awakening, so we keep the architectural image (builder, rafters, ridgepole) exact and let the verse land with the force of a victory cry.

divergences.phrase: my mind has reached the unmade, the unconditioned, Nirvana; I have come to the end of craving
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the mind, approaching the Eternal (visankhara, nirvana), has attained to the extinction of all desires."
divergences.lectio: We render visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ taṇhānaṃ khayam ajjhagā as "my mind has reached the unmade, the unconditioned, Nirvana; I have come to the end of craving," choosing "the unconditioned" for visaṅkhāra rather than Müller's "the Eternal," and "the end of craving" for taṇhānaṃ khaya rather than the vaguer "extinction of all desires."
divergences.note: Visaṅkhāra is the "un-constructed" or unconditioned — that which is not put together out of formations (saṅkhāra), a standard epithet of Nibbāna; "the Eternal" smuggles in a different metaphysic. And taṇhā is specifically craving, the very "house-builder" of the verse before, so the climax names its end exactly: the mind has reached the unmade, and craving is finished. We keep "Nirvana" alongside, as the Pali tradition glosses it.

divergences.phrase: the body is a fortress built of bones, plastered over with flesh and blood
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "After a stronghold has been made of the bones, it is covered with flesh and blood, and there dwell in it old age and death, pride and deceit."
divergences.lectio: We tighten Müller's two-step ("a stronghold has been made … it is covered") into a single image — "a fortress built of bones and plastered over with flesh and blood" — keeping aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ (a city/fortress of bones) and the grim tenants who dwell within: old age and death, pride and deceit.
divergences.note: The Pali aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ kataṃ maṃsalohitalepanaṃ pictures the body as a walled city framed of bone and daubed over with flesh and blood, housing jarā ca maccu ca māno makkho ca — aging, death, pride, and contempt/hypocrisy. "Plastered" keeps the literal lepana (a smearing-over, a coat of plaster), which makes the body's solidity look like a thin daubed shell, the point of this chapter's hard look at the flesh.

divergences.phrase: You are your own master; who else could be?
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali attā hi attano nātho / ko hi nātho paro siyā as "You are your own master; who else could be?" turning Müller's abstract third-person aphorism into direct address, and translate nātho as "master" (the one in charge, the refuge and protector) rather than the feudal "lord."
divergences.note: The Pali nātha means lord, protector, refuge — the one you can rely on — and the verse's punch is that this can only be yourself. Müller's "lord" and the doubled "self … self" read as Victorian and abstract; "you are your own master" keeps the exact sense (you are the one responsible for and capable of saving yourself) while letting the proverb land as the second-person challenge the Pali makes it.

divergences.phrase: grinds the fool down as a diamond grinds the gem it was cut from
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "The evil done by oneself, self-begotten, self-bred, crushes the foolish, as a diamond breaks a precious stone."
divergences.lectio: We keep the diamond simile but restore the force of vajiraṃ va smamayaṃ maniṃ — a diamond grinding the very stone-gem it was born from — so the picture mirrors the verse's point that self-made evil destroys the self that made it.
divergences.note: The Pali calls the diamond smamaya, "stone-born" — itself a hardened gem — and has it grind (abhimatthati) another gem of the same stuff. That parallel is the whole figure: just as the diamond is born of stone and yet wears stone away, so the fool's evil is self-begotten (attajaṃ attasambhavaṃ) and yet wears the fool away. Müller's "breaks a precious stone" loses the self-from-self mirroring; "grinds the gem it was cut from" keeps it without adding anything not in the Pali.

divergences.phrase: By yourself you are stained … by yourself you are made pure; no one can purify another
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali saṃkilissati as "you are stained" (defiled, made impure) rather than Müller's "one suffers," so the verse holds its single image of purity and impurity from the first line to the last, and put it in direct address to match the chapter's voice.
divergences.note: The Pali attanā va kataṃ pāpaṃ attanā saṃkilissati pairs "the wrong is done by oneself" with "by oneself one is defiled" — saṃkilissati is to be stained or polluted, the exact opposite of visujjhati, "is purified," in the next clause. Müller's "one suffers" breaks that pairing and weakens the verse's famous conclusion that purity and impurity are wholly one's own. "Stained / made pure" keeps the single thread, and the closing line — no one can purify another — is preserved word for word in sense.

divergences.phrase: the adept travel through the air by their own spiritual power
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "they go through the ether by means of their miraculous power"
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali ākāse yanti iddhiyā as "travel through the air by their own spiritual power," naming iddhi as the meditative attainment it is, rather than Müller's vague "miraculous power" and archaic "ether."
divergences.note: Iddhi is one of the higher knowledges (abhiññā) won through deep meditation — the power to move through space — not a generic "miracle." The verse sets three images side by side: the swan keeps to the sun's track, the adept passes through the air by iddhi, and the wise pass out of the world altogether by conquering Mara. "Spiritual power" keeps the technical sense; "ether" is dropped as dead Victorian science.

divergences.phrase: conquered Mara and all his army
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "when they have conquered Mara and his train"
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali māraṃ savāhiniṃ as "Mara and all his army" rather than Müller's "Mara and his train."
divergences.note: Savāhinī means "together with his host/army" — Mara, the King of Death, marshaled with his forces, the standard image of the tempter's whole array drawn up for battle. "Train" now reads as a retinue or a trailing robe and loses the martial force; "army" keeps the picture of the wise winning the field against death itself, and preserves the proper noun Mara.

divergences.phrase: the fruit of the first step into the stream
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the reward of the first step in holiness"
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali sotāpattiphalaṃ as "the fruit of the first step into the stream," keeping the river image of stream-entry that Müller flattens into the abstract "first step in holiness."
divergences.note: Sotāpatti is the technical first stage of awakening — literally "entering the stream" (sota, stream + āpatti, entering); one who reaches it is a sotāpanna, "one who has entered the stream," certain of Nirvana within a few more lives. Müller's "first step in holiness" loses the concrete metaphor and the doctrinal precision. "The first step into the stream" keeps the water image — and chimes with the far-shore crossing of chapter VI — without naming the technical term inside the verse.

divergences.phrase: the safe refuge—the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the Four Noble Truths
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "He who takes refuge with Buddha, the Law, and the Church; he who, with clear understanding, sees the four holy truths:—viz. pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain;—that is the safe refuge."
divergences.lectio: We keep the famous structure intact but restore the Buddhist terms the Pali names directly: the Dhamma (the Law) and the Sangha (the Order) for Müller's vaguer "the Law and the Church," and render the Four Noble Truths as suffering, its cause, its ending, and the Noble Eightfold Path—not the abstract "pain" and "quieting of pain."
divergences.note: The Pali (Buddhaṃ dhammaṃ ca saṅghaṃ ca … cattāri ariyasaccāni) names the three refuges and the four truths that are the doctrinal heart of the whole tradition. "Church" wrongly imports a Christian institution for saṅgha, the monastic community; "Order" is the standard rendering. Müller's dukkha as "pain" is too narrow—dukkha is suffering, unsatisfactoriness, the whole ache of conditioned existence. We hold the refuge verses and the four truths complete and explicit, since this is the passage the chapter exists for.

divergences.phrase: Not to do any evil, to cultivate good, to purify one's mind—this is the teaching of all the Buddhas
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
divergences.lectio: We keep this most central of all Buddhist summaries hard and plain: "Not to do any evil, to cultivate good, to purify one's own mind." We avoid "sin," which carries a Christian weight the Pali pāpa (evil, harm, the unwholesome) does not, and render kusalassa upasampadā as "to cultivate good" rather than the flat "to do good."
divergences.note: The Pali sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā, sacittapariyodapanaṃ is the verse Buddhists call the summary of the whole teaching. Akaraṇa is the not-doing, the active restraint, of all pāpa; upasampadā is the taking-up, the cultivating and full undertaking, of the wholesome (kusala); sacittapariyodapana is the cleansing of one's own mind. "Sin" mistranslates pāpa by importing guilt before a god; "evil" keeps it as harmful, unwholesome action. We preserve the threefold shape exactly so the line reads as the memorable creed it is.

divergences.phrase: Patience is the highest austerity; Nirvana is the highest, say the Buddhas
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "The Awakened call patience the highest penance, long-suffering the highest Nirvana."
divergences.lectio: We separate the two sayings the Pali keeps distinct: patience and endurance are the highest austerity, and—as a saying of its own—"Nirvana is the highest," say the Buddhas. Müller's "long-suffering the highest Nirvana" wrongly fuses them into one phrase.
divergences.note: The Pali reads khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā: "Patience, forbearance, is the highest austerity; the Buddhas say Nirvana is the highest." These are two parallel declarations—one about the highest practice (patient endurance, not bodily self-torture, is the true tapas), the other about the highest goal (Nibbana). Müller's reading makes "long-suffering" modify "Nirvana," losing the second clause's force as the Buddhas' verdict on the supreme end. We restore both as the Pali has them, and keep titikkhā (endurance) alongside khantī (patience).

divergences.phrase: no losing throw like hatred
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "there is no losing throw like hatred; there is no pain like this body."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's "losing throw" for the Pali kali — the unlucky cast of the dice — but restore khandha as "the burden of body and mind" rather than flattening it to "this body."
divergences.note: The Pali natthi dosasamo kali names hatred as the ruinous throw in a game of dice, the move that loses everything; the gambling image is worth keeping. And n'atthi khandhādisā dukkhā points not to the physical body alone but to the five khandhas — the whole bundle of form, feeling, perception, impulse, and consciousness that we take to be a self. "The burden of body and mind" keeps the doctrinal weight that Müller's "this body" loses, without naming the technical term mid-verse.

divergences.phrase: the things we are made of are the worst of burdens
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the body the greatest of pains."
divergences.lectio: We render saṅkhāra as "the things we are made of" — the conditioned, put-together stuff of existence — rather than narrowing it, as Müller does, to "the body."
divergences.note: Saṅkhārā are all conditioned, fabricated things: everything that is compounded and therefore impermanent, the whole machinery of becoming. The verse pairs hunger, the worst recurring affliction of the body, with saṅkhāra, the deeper affliction of being conditioned at all — which is why the cure named in the next breath is Nirvana, the unconditioned. "The body" loses that arc; "the things we are made of" keeps the contrast between the conditioned and the peace beyond it.

divergences.phrase: a trusted friend the best of kin
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "trust is the best of relationships."
divergences.lectio: We read vissāsaparamā ñātī as "a trusted friend the best of kin" rather than the abstract "trust is the best of relationships," keeping ñātī (kinsfolk, relatives) as a person, not a relationship.
divergences.note: The Pali ñātī means kin, blood relatives; the verse's four-fold proverb sets a concrete best against each category — best gain, best wealth, best kinsman, best happiness. Vissāsa is trust, confidence, intimacy, so vissāsaparamā ñātī is the one you can fully trust, who counts as the truest relative of all. Müller's "trust is the best of relationships" abstracts a person into a quality and breaks the parallel; "a trusted friend the best of kin" restores it, and chimes with verse 207's "welcome of kin."

divergences.phrase: From what is dear comes grief and fear
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "From pleasure comes grief" (212), "From affection" (213), "From lust" (214), "From love" (215), "From greed" (216).
divergences.lectio: We restore the five Pali terms in order—piya (the dear/beloved), pema (affection), rati (attachment, delight), kāma (lust, sensuality), taṇhā (craving)—so the chain climbs from ordinary fondness to the root craving the whole book is about, rather than Müller's looser "pleasure / affection / lust / love / greed."
divergences.note: The Pali repeats one frame five times, changing only the first word: piyato, pemato, ratiyā, kāmato, taṇhāya jāyatī soko. Müller's renderings drift—his "pleasure" for piya misses that piya is what one holds dear, his "love" for kāma is really sensual lust, and his "greed" for taṇhā hides the central term craving. We keep the five distinct and in their true order so the ladder of attachment is exact and the refrain rings the same each time.

divergences.phrase: so where would fear come from?
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear."
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali's rhetorical question—natthi soko kuto bhayaṃ, "there is no grief, so from where fear?"—rather than flattening it into a plain statement. The verse asks rather than asserts, and the question is the point.
divergences.note: Kuto bhayaṃ means literally "from where fear?"—a challenge, not a declaration. The logic is that once grief has no foothold, fear has nowhere to spring from. Müller's "knows neither grief nor fear" is accurate in sense but loses the verse's sharp turn; we keep the question so the proverb lands the way the Pali does.

divergences.phrase: a swimmer against the stream
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "he is called urdhvamsrotas (carried upwards by the stream)."
divergences.lectio: We render uddhaṃsoto as "a swimmer against the stream," the one who forges upstream against the current of craving toward Nirvana—not Müller's "carried upwards by the stream," which makes the current do the work.
divergences.note: Uddhaṃsota (Sanskrit ūrdhvaṃsrotas) is literally "upstream-going." The image is of one who swims hard against the world's downstream pull of sense-desire. Müller leaves the Sanskrit term untranslated and glosses it as being carried up by the stream, which inverts the effort the word names; the technical sense (a stage of the non-returner moving upward through the higher heavens) sits behind it, but the living image is the strong swimmer breasting the current, and we keep that.

divergences.phrase: as a driver reins in a runaway chariot
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali rathaṃ bhantaṃ va as "a runaway chariot" rather than Müller's neutral "a rolling chariot," so the simile carries its real force: anger is a chariot careering out of control, and only the one who can rein it in is a true driver.
divergences.note: The Pali bhanta means swerving, lurching, runaway—a chariot that has bolted, not one merely rolling along. The whole point is that controlling a vehicle already in motion takes no skill; mastering one that has gone wild is what makes a charioteer. "Rolling chariot" loses that danger; "runaway chariot" keeps it, and sharpens the contrast with those who only "hold the reins."

divergences.phrase: Overcome anger by calm, evil by good; overcome the miser by giving, the liar by truth
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali akkodhena jine kodhaṃ as "overcome anger by calm," keeping the literal sense of akkodha (non-anger, the absence of anger) rather than Müller's interpretive "by love," and plain up "the greedy by liberality" to "the miser by giving."
divergences.note: The famous fourfold remedy turns on opposites: anger met by akkodha (its own opposite, freedom from anger), evil by good, the stingy (kadariya) by giving, the liar by truth. Müller's "love" imports a warmer word than the Pali has and breaks the pattern of each fault cured by its exact contrary; "calm" keeps akkodha as the non-anger it literally names. The line is among the most quoted in the book, so we hold all four pairs intact and only free the diction.

divergences.phrase: worthy as a coin of the purest river-gold
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "like a coin made of gold from the Gambu river? Even the gods praise him, he is praised even by Brahman."
divergences.lectio: We render nikkhaṃ jambonadassa as "a coin of the purest river-gold," dropping Müller's transliterated "Gambu river," which means nothing to a modern reader, while keeping the image of finest gold and the closing line that even the gods—and Brahman himself—praise such a person.
divergences.note: Jambonada (jambūnada) gold is the legendary finest gold, said to come from the Jambu river; a nikkha is a weight or ornament or coin of it. Müller's "Gambu river" is a bare transliteration that conveys nothing; the point is simply gold of the highest purity, beyond all blame. We keep "river-gold" to preserve the image's origin without the opaque proper noun, and preserve Brahman by name, as the verse climaxes on the praise of the gods and of Brahman himself.

divergences.phrase: rust, springing from the iron itself, eats away the very iron that bred it
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "As the impurity which springs from the iron, when it springs from it, destroys it; thus do a transgressor's own works lead him to the evil path."
divergences.lectio: We name the impurity plainly as "rust" and keep the Pali's mirror exact—the iron is eaten away by what its own substance produces—so the simile lands as the picture of self-destruction it is.
divergences.note: The Pali ayasā va malaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ, taduṭṭhāya tam eva khādati: rust (mala) arises out of the iron (ayasā) and then devours the iron that gave it birth. The verse's force is that the corruption is self-bred and self-consuming—exactly as the wrongdoer's own deeds (sakakammāni) lead him to ruin. Müller's abstract "impurity … destroys it" loses the concrete rust-and-iron image; "the very iron that bred it" keeps the self-from-self mirroring the Pali draws.

divergences.phrase: ignorance is the greatest taint of all
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "But there is a taint worse than all taints,—ignorance is the greatest taint."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's wording almost intact, since it is already plain and forceful, and preserve "ignorance" for the Pali avijjā—the root unknowing the whole tradition names as the first link in the chain of suffering—rather than softening it to mere want of learning.
divergences.note: Avijjā is not simple lack of information but the deep not-seeing of how things are—the ignorance that heads the chain of dependent origination. The chapter has catalogued many taints (sloth, stinginess, misconduct, carelessness); here it names the one beneath them all. We hold the rhetorical climax exact—"worse than all these … the greatest taint of all"—and keep the technical term ignorance so the doctrinal point is not lost.

divergences.phrase: brazen as a crow
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Life is easy to live for a man who is without shame, a crow hero, a mischief-maker, an insulting, bold, and wretched fellow."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali kākasūra not by Müller's puzzling literal "crow hero" but by its plain sense—brazen, bold, and pushy as a crow—so the image reads as the insult it is rather than as a riddle.
divergences.note: Kākasūra (kāka, crow + sūra, hero/brave) is an idiom: a person as shameless and pushy as a scavenging crow, who shoves in anywhere and takes what it wants without embarrassment. "Crow hero" is a calque that means nothing to a modern reader; "brazen as a crow" keeps the bird and the brass. We pair it with the verse's other charges—shameless (ahirika), meddling, slanderous, insolent, corrupt—and let verse 245 set the modest life against it.

divergences.phrase: You are not just because you settle a case in haste
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "A man is not just if he carries a matter by violence; no, he who distinguishes both right and wrong... not by violence, but by law and equity... he is called just."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali yenatthaṃ sahasā naye as "settle a case in haste" rather than Müller's "carries a matter by violence," and keep dhamma as "what is right" / "established in dhamma" rather than the legalistic "law and equity."
divergences.note: The Pali sahasā means rashly, hastily, arbitrarily—deciding a lawsuit on impulse rather than weighing it; the verse was spoken of corrupt judges. Müller's "violence" reaches for the rarer sense of sahasa (force) and misses the point, which is that hasty, partial judgment is what makes a judge unjust. Dhammaṭṭha is "one who stands in dhamma," so we keep "established in dhamma" to chime with the chapter's title (Dhammaṭṭhavagga) rather than flattening dhamma to civil "law."

divergences.phrase: who does no harm
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "He in whom there is truth, virtue, love, restraint, moderation... he is called an elder."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali ahiṃsā as "does no harm" rather than Müller's "love." The word is not affection but non-violence—the refusal to injure any living thing—which is the precise virtue the chapter returns to in verse 270.
divergences.note: Ahiṃsā is literally "non-harming," the cardinal Buddhist (and Indian) virtue of doing no injury, and it is the same root that names the noble one (ariya) in verse 270, who is noble exactly because he harms no living creature. Müller's "love" softens and blurs it into a warm feeling; "does no harm" keeps the active restraint the Pali means and ties the true elder of 261 to the true noble of 270.

divergences.phrase: holds up the scales and chooses the good
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the wise who, taking the balance, chooses the good and avoids evil, he is a Muni... he who in this world weighs both sides is called a Muni."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's scales but plain the diction—"holds up the scales and chooses the good and turns away from evil"—and preserve the term muni as "sage," set against the false sage who is merely silent.
divergences.note: The Pali na monena muni hoti turns on a pun: mona (silence) does not make a muni (sage). The verse answers ascetics who claimed sagehood by keeping silent. The image is a merchant holding up a balance (tulaṃ va paggayha) to weigh good against evil and take the better—discernment, not mere quiet, is what makes the sage. We keep the scales exact and hold "sage" steady for muni so the wordplay and the chapter's "not merely by X is one truly Y" pattern both land.

divergences.phrase: All conditioned things are impermanent … suffering … without a self—when you see this with wisdom, you turn away from suffering
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "'All created things perish' … 'All created things are grief and pain' … 'All forms are unreal,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity."
divergences.lectio: We restore the three marks as the Pali names them and keeps them parallel: sabbe sankhara anicca (impermanent), sabbe sankhara dukkha (suffering), sabbe dhamma anatta (without self), each closing on the refrain "you turn away from suffering; this is the path to purity."
divergences.note: These three verses are the doctrinal core of the chapter—the tilakkhana, the three marks of existence. Müller's "all forms are unreal" for sabbe dhamma anatta is wrong: anatta is "without self," not "unreal," and dhamma here is all things, not "forms." His "becomes passive in pain" mistranslates atha nibbindati dukkhe—nibbindati is to grow weary of, to turn away in disenchantment from, suffering. We keep the Pali terms in parentheses and the refrain identical across all three so the marks read as the matched triad the Pali makes them.

divergences.phrase: Of all paths, the Eightfold Path is the best
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see."
divergences.lectio: We name the doctrinal terms the verse points to—the Noble Eightfold Path and the Four Noble Truths—rather than Müller's bare "eightfold" and his opaque "four words," and render virago (passionlessness) as "freedom from craving," the book's central theme.
divergences.note: The Pali maggan' atthangiko settho, saccanam caturo pada sets the supreme path (the Eightfold Path) beside the supreme truth (the Four Noble Truths, the "four words/states"), the supreme state (viraga, dispassion, freedom from raga/craving), and the supreme person (the one with eyes to see, the Buddha). Müller's "four words" is a literal but baffling rendering of caturo pada; naming the Four Noble Truths makes the verse's claim plain without adding anything not in the Pali.

divergences.phrase: Cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree—for out of that forest comes fear
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Cut down the whole forest (of lust), not a tree only! Danger comes out of the forest (of lust)."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's forest image exactly but free its diction—"forest of desire" for vana, "fear" for the Pali bhaya rather than "danger"—and preserve the wordplay the verse turns on between vana (forest) and the undergrowth that must also be cleared.
divergences.note: The Pali vanam chindatha ma rukkham, vanato jayate bhayam puns on vana, which means both "forest" and "desire/craving"—so "cut down the forest, not just one tree" is at once a literal felling and the uprooting of craving entire, not one craving at a time. From that forest comes bhaya, fear (the dread bound up with attachment). We hold the image and its double sense intact—forest and undergrowth (vana and vanatha)—so the proverb lands as the Pali makes it, and keep the famous line "cut down the forest of desire."

divergences.phrase: Having killed mother and father and two kings … the true Brahmin goes on his way unharmed
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "A true Brahmana goes scatheless, though he have killed father and mother, and two valiant kings, though he has destroyed a kingdom with all its subjects."
divergences.lectio: We keep the deliberate shock of the Pali intact—mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā—rendering it plainly as "having killed mother and father and two kings," and translate anīgho yāti brāhmaṇo as "the true Brahmin goes on his way unharmed," rather than the archaic "goes scatheless." We preserve the riddle without flattening it into a moral.
divergences.note: These verses are a deliberate paradox: the commentary glosses mother as craving (taṇhā), father as the conceit "I am" (asmimāna), the two kings as the views of eternalism and annihilationism, and the kingdom with its treasurer (or, in 295, its "tiger," the hindrance of doubt) as the twelve sense-bases and attachment. The arahat who has destroyed all these goes free of suffering. We keep the verse's startling literal surface—as the Pali does—rather than dissolving it into the allegory, since the shock is the point and the gloss belongs in the margin, not the line.

divergences.phrase: painful it is to keep wandering on … so do not be a wanderer who is hounded by that pain
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the itinerant mendicant is beset with pain. Therefore let no man be an itinerant mendicant and he will not be beset with pain."
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali addhagū to its proper sense—"a wayfarer," one who travels on through saṃsāra—rather than Müller's "itinerant mendicant." The verse does not advise against being a monk; it counts up the pains of every state of life and urges the reader not to remain a traveler on the endless road of rebirth.
divergences.note: Müller reads dukkho 'naddhāna­saṃvāso … tasmā na c'addhagū siyā as a warning against the wandering monk's life, which contradicts the whole book's praise of the homeless path. The standard reading takes addhagū as one who journeys the long road of birth and death (addhāna, the road/the round): companionship with what does not pass is painful, and to be a perpetual traveler on that round is to be hounded by suffering—so end the journey. We follow the received Pali against Müller's inverted sense.

divergences.phrase: the taints keep on growing … the taints come to an end
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the desires of unruly, thoughtless people are always increasing" … "the desires of such watchful and wise people will come to an end."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali āsavā as "the taints" rather than the vaguer "desires," keeping the technical term for the deep defilements that flood the mind, and translate kāyagatā sati as being "mindful of the body" directly.
divergences.note: Āsava (literally an outflow, a fermenting influx) names the basic taints—sensual craving, becoming, views, and ignorance—whose ending is liberation itself; "desires" narrows and weakens this. The contrast of the chapter is exact: in the heedless the āsavas swell, while in those grounded in mindfulness of the body (kāyagatā sati, a specific meditation) they dry up. We keep "the taints" so the verse names the very thing the path exists to end.

divergences.phrase: Better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, blazing like fire, than to live on the alms of the land while being immoral and undisciplined
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Better it would be to swallow a heated iron ball, like flaring fire, than that a bad unrestrained fellow should live on the charity of the land."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's terrible image exact but free its diction—"red-hot iron ball" for "heated iron ball," "the alms of the land" for "the charity of the land"—and turn the third-person "a bad unrestrained fellow" into the plain charge of being immoral and undisciplined.
divergences.note: The Pali seyyo ayoguḷo bhutto, tatto aggisikhūpamo, than that a dussīlo (immoral, of broken virtue) should eat raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ, the country's alms-food, makes the point that to take the laity's offerings while breaking the precepts is worse than swallowing molten iron. "Charity of the land" sounds like welfare; "the alms of the land" keeps the picture of the monk fed by the people he is failing. The iron ball is the chapter's most famous image, so we hold it whole.

divergences.phrase: only the brief pleasure of one frightened soul in the arms of another
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "the short pleasure of the frightened in the arms of the frightened."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's striking phrase but plain it up—"one frightened soul in the arms of another"—so the picture of two people stealing a guilty, fearful moment reads clearly rather than as a riddle of repeated abstractions.
divergences.note: The Pali bhayā bhayaratī ca thokikā names the fleeting, fear-ridden pleasure of the adulterer and the woman, both glancing over their shoulders—frightened of discovery, of the husband, of the king's rod. "The frightened in the arms of the frightened" is faithful but stiff; "one frightened soul in the arms of another" keeps both parties afraid and the pleasure brief, without inventing anything the Pali does not have.

divergences.phrase: the monk's life, wrongly lived, drags a man down to hell
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "badly-practised asceticism leads to hell."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ as "the monk's life, wrongly lived" rather than the broad "badly-practised asceticism," since sāmañña is specifically the life of the recluse (samaṇa), and keep the active force of pakaḍḍhati—"drags down"—against Müller's milder "leads."
divergences.note: The simile is exact and physical: kuso duggahito, a blade of kusa grass grasped the wrong way, cuts the hand that holds it; so sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ, the monastic life taken up the wrong way, hauls one down to niraya. "Asceticism" widens the verse to self-mortification in general; the Pali is about the monk who wears the robe but lives loosely—the same figure as verse 307. "Drags a man down" keeps pakaḍḍhati's image of being hauled by force, not gently led.

divergences.phrase: the untrodden country, Nirvana
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "For with these animals does no man reach the untrodden country (Nirvana), where a tamed man goes on a tamed animal, viz. on his own well-tamed self."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's vivid "untrodden country" for the Pali agataṁ disaṁ and hold the wordplay of the last line intact—"tamed, riding his own well-tamed self"—while smoothing his clogged "viz. on his own well-tamed self."
divergences.note: The Pali agataṁ disaṁ is literally "the region not gone to," the place no ordinary traveler has ever reached, a standing image for Nibbana; danto dantena gacchati turns on danta (tamed), so the self-tamed person rides to the goal on the only mount that can carry anyone there—his own tamed self. "Untrodden country" keeps that picture; we drop the Victorian "viz." so the verse reads as one clean line.

divergences.phrase: his temples streaming in must
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "his temples running with sap, and difficult to hold, does not eat a morsel when bound; the elephant longs for the elephant grove."
divergences.lectio: We render the Pali kaṭukabhedano (the rut-fluid breaking from the temples) as "his temples streaming in must," the proper term for a bull elephant in heat, rather than Müller's vague "running with sap," and keep Dhanapalaka by name and the elephant's longing for the grove exact.
divergences.note: A male elephant in musth (Pali: the temporal glands breaking and flowing) is wild and uncontrollable; the captured Dhanapalaka refuses food, pining for the freedom of the elephant-grove. "Running with sap" obscures the image, since the fluid is the elephant's own rut, not tree-sap. "Must/musth" is the exact English word for the condition and keeps the verse's picture of a powerful creature that cannot be held and will not be consoled in captivity.

divergences.phrase: a Matanga elephant roaming the forest
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "like an elephant in the forest" (329, 330), dropping the Pali mātaṅga.
divergences.lectio: We restore the Pali mātaṅgaraññe va nāgo as "a Matanga elephant roaming the forest," keeping the proper epithet Matanga that names the great solitary forest bull, rather than Müller's plain "an elephant in the forest."
divergences.note: Mātaṅga is a name and title for the noble lone elephant of the wild—the tusker who has left the herd and ranges the forest alone, the very image the verse holds up for one who must walk the path without a worthy companion. Müller flattens it to a generic "elephant"; preserving "Matanga" keeps the dignity and the proper noun the Pali chooses, and ties the solitary walker of 329-330 back to the named Dhanapalaka of 324 and the chapter's whole elephant imagery.

divergences.phrase: his sorrows grow like grass after rain … fall away like water-drops from a lotus leaf
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "his sufferings increase like the abounding Birana grass" … "sufferings fall off from him, like water-drops from a lotus leaf."
divergences.lectio: We keep both of the chapter's famous images intact but free their diction: "grow thick and fast, like wild grass after rain" for the obscure "abounding Birana grass," and "slide off a lotus leaf" for "fall off … from a lotus leaf."
divergences.note: The Pali bīraṇa is a specific wild grass that springs up rank and fast once it takes hold; the name means nothing to a modern reader, so we render the picture (fast-spreading weed-grass) rather than transliterating it. The lotus-leaf image (udabindu va pokkharā) is one of the most loved in the book—water that cannot wet the leaf, just as sorrow cannot cling to the one who has conquered craving—so we keep it exact and only smooth the verb.

divergences.phrase: cut his way out of the thicket of craving, only to run straight back into it
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "He who having got rid of the forest (of lust) (i.e. after having reached Nirvana) gives himself over to forest-life (i.e. to lust), and who, when removed from the forest (i.e. from lust), runs to the forest (i.e. to lust), look at that man! though free, he runs into bondage."
divergences.lectio: We let the verse's own wordplay carry the meaning instead of breaking it open with four parenthetical glosses. The Pali turns on vana (thicket/forest) doubling as craving; we render the whole image as a man who hacks free of the thicket and then runs back into it, "set free, runs back into bondage of his own accord."
divergences.note: The Pali yo nibbanatho vanādhimutto, vanamutto vanam-eva dhāvati puns relentlessly on vana (forest) and vanatha (undergrowth), both of which also mean craving—so the literal picture (a man freed from the woods who bolts straight back) is the metaphor (a man freed from craving who returns to it). Müller's text stops the line dead with "(i.e. to lust)" four times; we trust the reader to feel the pun, keep the single clean image of someone who frees himself only to re-enter bondage, and move the gloss to the margin where it belongs.

divergences.phrase: skilled in language and its meanings, who knows how words are formed and ordered
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "who understands the words and their interpretation, who knows the order of letters (those which are before and which are after)."
divergences.lectio: We render niruttipadakovido as "skilled in language and its meanings" and the puzzling "order of letters, those before and after" as "how words are formed and ordered," naming the linguistic skill the verse actually praises rather than leaving Müller's near-nonsensical literalism on the page.
divergences.note: Niruttipada is the analytic knowledge of language—etymology, usage, the way words are built and combined (one of the four kinds of discriminating insight, paṭisambhidā). Müller's "the order of letters, those which are before and which are after" is a word-for-word calque (pubbāparāni akkharāni) that reads as a riddle; the sense is mastery of how words are formed and arranged. We keep it plain so the verse's point—that the great sage is also a master of language and meaning—comes through, and hold "craving" steady for taṇhā at the head of the line.

divergences.phrase: The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts … the end of craving conquers all sorrow
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "The gift of the law exceeds all gifts; the sweetness of the law exceeds all sweetness; the delight in the law exceeds all delights; the extinction of thirst overcomes all pain."
divergences.lectio: We restore the term Dhamma for Müller's flattened "the law," render rasa as "taste" rather than "sweetness," and translate taṇhakkhayo as "the end of craving" overcoming "all sorrow" rather than "the extinction of thirst" over "pain."
divergences.note: This is the chapter's most quoted verse (sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti…). Dhamma is the teaching itself, not civil "law"; we keep the proper term as we do throughout the book. Rasa is taste/flavor, so "the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes" holds the fourfold parallel exact (gift, taste, delight, conquest). And taṇhakkhaya is precisely "the end of craving," the goal the whole chapter drives at, conquering dukkha—sorrow, suffering—not merely "pain."

divergences.phrase: Cut off five, let go of five, and cultivate five more
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Cut off the five (senses), leave the five, rise above the five."
divergences.lectio: We drop Müller's parenthetical gloss "(senses)," which is mistaken. The three fives are not the senses but the five lower fetters (to be cut off), the five higher fetters (to be let go), and the five faculties — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (to be cultivated). We render uttari bhavaye plainly as "cultivate five more."
divergences.note: The Pali pañca chinde pañca jahe pañca cuttari bhavaye names three distinct sets of five, as the commentarial tradition makes clear: chinde (cut off) the five lower fetters — self-view, doubt, clinging to rites, sensual desire, ill will; jahe (abandon) the five higher fetters — craving for form realms, craving for formless realms, conceit, restlessness, ignorance; and bhavaye (cultivate) the five spiritual faculties. Müller's "(senses)" collapses all three into the sense-faculties and loses the verse's whole architecture; the monk who masters all fifteen is the pañcasaṅgātiga, one who has gone beyond the five attachments and so has "crossed the flood" (oghatiṇṇa) of samsara.

divergences.phrase: There is no meditation for one without wisdom, and no wisdom for one who does not meditate
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge."
divergences.lectio: We render paññā as "wisdom" rather than Müller's flatter "knowledge," and keep jhāna as "meditation," so the famous reciprocal proverb names the two faculties the tradition pairs — and reverse Müller's clause order to put meditation first, matching the Pali natthi jhānaṃ apaññassa.
divergences.note: The Pali natthi jhānaṃ apaññassa, paññā natthi ajhāyato; yamhi jhānañ ca paññā ca, sa ve nibbānasantike turns on the two great wings of the path: jhāna (meditative absorption, the stilling and gathering of the mind) and paññā (wisdom, the seeing into things as they are). Each depends on the other, and only where both are present does one stand "in the presence of Nirvana." Müller's "knowledge" understates paññā, which is liberating insight, not information; "wisdom" keeps the doctrinal weight and the proverb's balance.

divergences.phrase: Empty this boat, O monk!
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "O Bhikshu, empty this boat! if emptied, it will go quickly."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's celebrated image almost intact, only freeing the diction — "Empty this boat" and "it will move swiftly" — and rendering rāga as "craving" rather than his "passion," so the term stays tied to the book's central theme.
divergences.note: The Pali siñca bhikkhu imaṃ nāvaṃ, sittā te lahum essati pictures the body as a boat shipping water: bail it out — empty it of the wrong thoughts and defilements pooling within — and lightened, it will sail swiftly. The water cut off is named in the next breath: rāga (craving) and dosa (hatred), the two afflictions whose removal carries one to Nirvana. "Passion" blurs rāga, the technical desire/craving the whole book turns on; "craving" keeps the thread, and we hold the boat-and-water image exact, since it is one of the best-loved figures in the text.

divergences.phrase: Knowing the destruction of all that is made, you will know the Uncreated, Nirvana
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "When you have understood the destruction of all that was made, you will understand that which was not made."
divergences.lectio: We keep Müller's made/unmade antithesis but name the unmade plainly as the Uncreated, Nirvana, so the chapter—and the whole book—opens its finale on the goal itself rather than an abstraction the modern reader will miss.
divergences.note: The Pali saṅkhārānaṃ khayaṃ ñatvā akataññū'si brāhmaṇa turns on saṅkhāra (the made, the conditioned, all that is put together) against akata (the un-made, the unconditioned)—a standard epithet of Nibbāna. Müller's bare "that which was not made" is faithful but opaque; we keep the contrast and let "the Uncreated, Nirvana" carry the meaning, as the Pali tradition glosses akata. "Cut off the stream" keeps chinda sotaṃ, the stream of craving whose cutting makes one a stream-enterer.

divergences.phrase: Not by matted hair, not by lineage, not by birth does one become a Brahmin; the one in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is the Brahmin
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana."
divergences.lectio: We render jaṭā as "matted hair" rather than the archaic "platted hair," and hold the verse's revolutionary claim hard and plain: a Brahmin is made not by birth or caste but by truth (sacca) and righteousness (dhamma). This is the doctrinal heart of the whole chapter, so we let it land without softening.
divergences.note: The Pali na jaṭāhi na gottena na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo / yamhi saccañ ca dhammo ca so sucī so ca brāhmaṇo overturns the Brahmin caste-claim by birth (jacca) and lineage (gotta): the true Brahmin is whoever holds truth and dhamma, of any birth. This was the Buddha's direct challenge to the caste order, spoken to Jaṭila the matted-haired ascetic who claimed Brahmin status by blood. "Matted hair" keeps the concrete picture of the ascetic's locks; "truth and righteousness" keeps sacca and dhamma exact, and the whole chapter's redefinition of "Brahmin" by attainment rather than birth depends on this verse reading clean.

divergences.phrase: no more than water clings to a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed clings to the point of a needle
divergences.older: Müller (1881): "who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle" (401); "have dropt like a mustard seed from the point of a needle" (407).
divergences.lectio: We keep both of the chapter's famous non-clinging images exact—water that will not stay on the lotus leaf, the mustard seed that will not rest on the needle's point—but turn them into the active verb "clings" so the picture states its own meaning: the liberated one holds to nothing, and nothing holds to him.
divergences.note: The Pali vāri pokkharapatte va, āragge-r-iva sāsapo pictures water beading and rolling off a lotus leaf and a tiny mustard seed that cannot balance on a needle's tip—both images of perfect non-adhesion. The same needle-point figure returns in 407 for anger and pride falling away. These are among the book's most loved similes for non-attachment, so we hold them concrete and let "clings" carry the doctrinal point (taṇhā, craving, finds no purchase) without an abstraction.

segments.text: 1. All that we are is shaped by what we have thought. The mind goes before everything; the mind makes everything; everything is made of the mind. If you speak or act with a corrupted mind, suffering follows you, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that pulls the cart.

2. All that we are is shaped by what we have thought. The mind goes before everything; the mind makes everything; everything is made of the mind. If you speak or act with a clear mind, happiness follows you, like a shadow that never leaves.
3. "He insulted me, he struck me, he beat me, he robbed me"—in those who hold on to such thoughts, hatred never ends.
4. "He insulted me, he struck me, he beat me, he robbed me"—in those who let go of such thoughts, hatred comes to an end.
5. Hatred is never ended by hatred. Hatred ends only by love—this is the ancient and unchanging law.
6. Most people never grasp that we are all bound to die here. But those who do grasp it lay down their quarrels at once.
7. Whoever lives chasing only pleasures, with his senses unguarded, eating without limit, lazy and weak—Mara, the tempter, will overthrow him as the wind overthrows a frail tree.
8. Whoever lives without chasing pleasures, with his senses well guarded, eating in moderation, faithful and strong—Mara will no more overthrow him than the wind can overthrow a mountain of rock.
9. Whoever puts on the saffron robe before he has cleansed himself of his own corruption, who has no self-restraint and no truth in him, is not worthy of the robe.
10. But whoever has cleansed himself of corruption, is firmly rooted in virtue, and holds to self-restraint and truth, he is truly worthy of the robe.
11. Those who take the false for the true, and see the true as false, never reach the truth; they wander after empty desires.
12. Those who know the true as true, and the false as false, do reach the truth; they follow desires that are real.
13. As rain breaks through a poorly thatched house, so craving breaks through an undisciplined mind.
14. As rain cannot break through a well-thatched house, so craving cannot break through a well-disciplined mind.
15. The wrongdoer grieves in this world and grieves in the next; in both he grieves. He grieves and suffers when he sees the harm his own deeds have done.
16. The good person rejoices in this world and rejoices in the next; in both he rejoices. He rejoices and is glad when he sees the good his own deeds have done.
17. The wrongdoer suffers in this world and suffers in the next; in both he suffers. He suffers knowing, "I have done wrong," and he suffers still more on the path that wrongdoing leads to.
18. The good person is happy in this world and happy in the next; in both he is happy. He is happy knowing, "I have done good," and he is happier still on the path that good leads to.
19. Though a heedless man can recite a great deal of the teaching, if he does not live by it he has no share in the holy life—he is like a hired cowherd counting another man's cattle.

20. Though a man can recite only a little of the teaching, if he lives by it—if he has let go of craving, hatred, and delusion, if he has true knowledge and a mind set free, clinging to nothing in this world or the next—he has a real share in the holy life.
21. Heedfulness is the path to the deathless; heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if already dead.
22. Seeing this clearly, the wise hold heedfulness above all else. They take their joy in heedfulness, delighting in the ground the Noble Ones walk.
23. These are the meditators, steady, unrelenting in their effort; and these are the ones, strong and clear-minded, who reach Nirvana, the highest freedom, the highest peace.
24. The one who has roused himself and stays awake, whose deeds are clean, who acts with care, who holds himself in check and lives by what is right and heedful — his good name only grows.
25. By rousing himself, by heedfulness, by self-mastery and self-control, let the wise build an island that no flood can wash away.
26. Fools, the slow-witted, give themselves over to carelessness. The wise guard their heedfulness as their most precious treasure.
27. Do not give yourself to carelessness; do not give yourself to the pleasures of desire. Heedful and absorbed in meditation, you will come into ample joy.

28. When the wise drive out carelessness by heedfulness, they climb the high terraces of wisdom and, free of sorrow, look down on the sorrowing crowd — as one standing on a mountain looks down on those who stand on the plain.
29. Heedful among the heedless, wide awake among the sleeping, the wise leave them far behind, like a swift horse leaving a slow one in its dust.
30. By heedfulness Indra rose to be lord of the gods. Heedfulness is forever praised; carelessness is forever blamed.
31. The monk who delights in heedfulness and dreads carelessness moves like a fire, burning away every fetter, small or great.
32. The monk who delights in heedfulness and dreads carelessness cannot fall back — he stands close upon Nirvana.
33. As an arrow-maker straightens his arrow, the wise straighten the mind — restless and unsteady, hard to guard, hard to hold back.
34. Like a fish pulled from the water and thrown on dry land, the mind thrashes and quivers as it struggles to escape the grip of Mara.
35. The mind is hard to hold down, light and quick, settling wherever it pleases. Good it is to tame it; a tamed mind brings happiness.
36. Let the wise watch over the mind, so hard to see, so subtle, settling wherever it pleases. A mind well guarded brings happiness.
37. The mind travels far, wanders alone, has no body, and hides in the cave of the heart. Those who keep it in check will be freed from the bonds of Mara.
38. If the mind is unsteady, if a person does not know the true teaching, if their peace is shaken, their wisdom will never come to fullness.
39. But for one whose mind is unshaken, untroubled, who has let go of both good and evil and stays awake, there is no fear.
