40. Knowing this body to be fragile as a clay jar, make the mind a fortress, and with the weapon of wisdom go to war against Mara — then guard what you have won, and never rest at ease.
41. Before long, alas, this body will lie on the ground, cast aside, empty of awareness, like a useless log.
42. Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to one he hates, a misdirected mind will do you far worse.
43. Not a mother, not a father, not any kin can do for you what a rightly directed mind can do — far greater is its gift.
44. Who will master this earth, and the realm of Death, and the world of the gods? Who will gather the well-taught path of virtue, as a skilled hand chooses the right flower?

45. The disciple in training will master this earth, and the realm of Death, and the world of the gods. The disciple will gather the well-taught path of virtue, as a skilled hand chooses the right flower.
46. Whoever knows that this body is like foam, and sees that it is as fleeting as a mirage, will snap the flower-tipped arrows of Mara and pass beyond the sight of the King of Death.
47. Death sweeps away the one who is busy gathering flowers, his mind elsewhere, as a flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
48. Death overpowers the one who is busy gathering flowers, his mind elsewhere, before he has had his fill of pleasure.
49. As the bee takes the nectar and flies off without harming the flower, its color, or its scent, so let the sage move through the village.
50. Let the sage not dwell on the faults of others, on what they have done or left undone, but only on what he himself has done or left undone.
51. Like a lovely flower, full of color but with no scent, are the fine words of one who speaks well but does not act.
52. But like a lovely flower, full of color and full of scent, are the fine words of one who speaks well and acts on them, and they bear fruit.
53. As many garlands can be woven from a heap of flowers, so should a mortal, once born, do many good things with this life.

54. The scent of flowers does not travel against the wind, nor the scent of sandalwood, of tagara, or of jasmine; but the fragrance of the good travels even against the wind. A good person reaches every quarter.
55. Sandalwood and tagara, the lotus and the jasmine — sweet as all these perfumes are, the fragrance of virtue surpasses them all.
56. Faint is the scent of tagara and sandalwood; but the fragrance of those who keep virtue is the finest of all, and it rises even to the gods.
57. Mara never finds the path of those who keep these virtues, who live in heedfulness, and who are set free by true knowledge.

58, 59. As on a heap of rubbish tossed by the roadside a lotus may grow, sweet-scented and a delight to the heart, so among the rubbish of blind and ordinary people the disciple of the truly awakened Buddha shines out in wisdom.
60. Long is the night to one who lies awake; long is the road to one who is weary; long is the round of rebirth to the fool who does not know the true teaching.
61. If on his journey a traveler meets no one better than himself, or even his equal, let him hold firmly to his solitary road; there is no companionship with a fool.
62. "These sons are mine, this wealth is mine"—with such thoughts the fool torments himself. He does not even belong to himself; how then can sons or wealth be his?
63. The fool who knows he is a fool is wise at least in that. But the fool who thinks himself wise—he is the fool indeed.
64. Even if a fool keeps company with a wise man all his life, he no more grasps the truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.
65. But if a clear-minded man keeps company with a wise man for even a moment, he grasps the truth at once, as the tongue tastes the flavor of the soup.
66. Fools, dull of understanding, are their own worst enemies, for they do evil deeds that bear bitter fruit.
67. That deed is not well done which a man regrets afterward, whose fruit he receives weeping, with tears on his face.
68. But that deed is well done which a man does not regret, whose fruit he receives gladly and with a glad heart.
69. As long as the evil deed has not yet ripened, the fool thinks it sweet as honey; but when it ripens, the fool comes to grief.
70. Month after month a fool may eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, like an ascetic—yet he is not worth a sixteenth part of those who have truly understood the teaching.
71. An evil deed does not curdle at once, like fresh milk; it follows the fool smoldering, like a fire hidden under ashes.
72. And when at last it comes to light, that evil deed brings the fool only sorrow; it shatters his good fortune and splits his very head.
73. Let the fool crave a reputation he has not earned, precedence among the monks, authority in the monasteries, and honor from people everywhere.
74. "Let both layfolk and monks think this was done by me; let them defer to me in all things, great and small"—such is the mind of the fool, and his craving and his pride only swell.
75. One road leads to worldly gain, another leads to Nirvana. Knowing this, let the monk, the follower of the Buddha, take no delight in honor, but give himself to solitude instead.

76. If you meet a discerning person who sees your faults and tells you of them, who shows you what to avoid and reproves you when you are wrong, follow that wise one as you would follow a guide to buried treasure. It will go better, never worse, for the one who follows him.
77. Let such a person counsel you, teach you, and hold you back from what is base. The good will love him for it; only the bad will hate him.
78. Do not make friends of those who do wrong; do not make friends of the mean and low. Make friends of the good; make friends of the best among people.
79. Whoever drinks deep of the teaching lives happily, with a mind at peace. The wise take joy, day after day, in the truth the Noble Ones have taught.
80. Farmers channel the water where they want it; arrow-makers straighten the shaft; carpenters shape the wood; and the wise shape themselves.
81. As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by praise or blame.
82. When the wise have listened to the teaching, they grow clear and still, like a lake that is deep, smooth, and undisturbed.
83. Good people let go wherever they are; they do not chatter on, hungry for pleasure. Touched by happiness or by sorrow, the wise show neither swelling joy nor sinking despair.
84. The one who would not, for his own sake or another's, crave a son, or wealth, or power, and who would not seek his own success by wrong means—that one is good, and wise, and upright.
85. Few among people ever cross to the other shore; the rest run up and down the near bank.
86. But those who follow the teaching, when it has been well taught to them, will cross beyond the reach of death, hard as that crossing is to make.
87. Leaving the dark way behind, let the wise take up the bright way. Let him go from home into homelessness, into the solitude that few find easy to enjoy.
88. There let him seek his joy, having given up every pleasure and called nothing his own. Let the wise cleanse himself of all that troubles the mind.

89. Those whose minds are firmly grounded in the factors of awakening, who cling to nothing and delight in letting go of all grasping, whose craving is mastered and who shine with light—they are set free, even here in this world.
90. For the one who has finished the journey, who has let go of grief, who is free on every side and has thrown off every chain, there is no more fever of pain.
91. The mindful keep moving; they take no comfort in settling down. Like swans that rise and leave the lake, they leave one resting place after another behind them.

92. They store up nothing; they understand the food they eat for what it is; their aim is emptiness, the freedom that depends on nothing—Nirvana. Their track cannot be followed, like the path of birds across the sky.

93. The one whose cravings are stilled, who is not caught in any pleasure, whose aim is emptiness, the freedom that depends on nothing—Nirvana—his track cannot be followed, like the path of birds across the sky.
94. Even the gods envy the one whose senses are calmed, like horses well broken by their driver, who has shed all pride and is free of every craving.

95. Such a one bears all things and resents nothing, like the earth; he stands firm, like the great threshold-pillar at the city gate; he is clear, like a deep pool with no mud to cloud it. For him there are no more births to come.
96. Quiet is the mind of such a one, quiet his words, quiet his deeds, for he has won his freedom through true knowledge and come to rest.
97. The one who takes nothing on blind faith but knows the uncreated for himself, who has cut every tie, ended every chance of rebirth, and thrown off every desire—he is the greatest of all.
98. In a village or in the forest, in the valley or on the hill, wherever the venerable ones dwell—there the ground is a delight.
99. Delightful are the forests where the crowd finds no delight. There those who are free of craving will be glad, for they are not looking for pleasures.
100. Better than a thousand words, if they are empty of sense, is the one word of sense that brings peace to whoever hears it.
101. Better than a thousand verses, if they are empty of sense, is the one line of verse that brings peace to whoever hears it.
102. Better than reciting a hundred verses empty of sense is the one word of the teaching that brings peace to whoever hears it.
103. Though a man should conquer a thousand thousand men in battle, the one who conquers himself is the greatest conqueror of all.
104. Victory over oneself is better than victory over anyone else. The man who has mastered himself and lives always under restraint—
105. not a god, not a Gandharva, not Mara, not even Brahman could turn his victory into defeat.

106. Though month after month for a hundred years a man should offer a thousand sacrifices, if for a single moment he honors one who has perfected himself, that homage is worth more than a hundred years of sacrifice.

107. Though for a hundred years a man should tend the sacred fire in the forest, if for a single moment he honors one who has perfected himself, that homage is worth more than a hundred years of worship.
108. Whatever a man offers or sacrifices in this world for a whole year to gain merit, all of it is not worth a quarter of the reverence shown to the upright; reverence to the upright is better.
109. To one who always honors and respects the elders, four things increase: long life, beauty, happiness, and strength.
110. Better than a hundred years lived in vice, with no self-control, is a single day lived in virtue and reflection.
111. Better than a hundred years lived in ignorance, with no self-control, is a single day lived in wisdom and reflection.
112. Better than a hundred years lived in idleness and weakness is a single day lived with firm and steady effort.
113. Better than a hundred years lived without ever seeing how all things rise and pass away is a single day in which you see them rise and pass away.
114. Better than a hundred years lived without ever seeing the deathless is a single day in which you see the deathless.
115. Better than a hundred years lived without ever seeing the highest law is a single day in which you see the highest law.
116. Be quick to do good, and hold your mind back from evil. The one who is slow to do good finds his mind taking its delight in evil.
117. If you do wrong, do not do it again; do not let your heart take pleasure in it. Heaping up evil ends in pain.
118. If you do good, do it again; let your heart take pleasure in it. Heaping up good ends in happiness.
119. Even the wrongdoer sees good days, as long as his evil has not yet ripened. But once that evil ripens, the wrongdoer meets his evil.
120. Even the good person sees hard days, as long as his good has not yet ripened. But once that good ripens, the good person meets his good days.
121. Do not think lightly of evil, telling yourself, "It will never come near me." Drop by drop the water-pot is filled; little by little the fool fills himself with evil.
122. Do not think lightly of good, telling yourself, "It will never come near me." Drop by drop the water-pot is filled; little by little the wise fill themselves with good.
123. Avoid evil deeds as a merchant carrying rich goods with few companions avoids a dangerous road, as one who loves life avoids poison.
124. A hand with no wound on it may carry poison unharmed, for poison cannot enter where there is no wound. In the same way, no evil touches the one who does no evil.
125. Whoever wrongs an innocent person—one who is harmless, pure, and blameless—the evil falls back on that fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.
126. Some are born again into the womb; those who do evil go to hell; those who do right go to heaven; and those who are free of every desire reach Nirvana.
127. Not in the sky, not in the middle of the sea, not deep in a mountain cave—nowhere in all the world is there a place where you can escape your own evil deed.
129. Everyone trembles at the rod; everyone is afraid of death. Knowing that others are just like yourself, do not kill, and do not make others kill.
130. Everyone trembles at the rod; everyone holds life dear. Knowing that others are just like yourself, do not kill, and do not make others kill.
131. Whoever, hunting his own happiness, harms with the rod other beings who long for happiness too, will find no happiness hereafter.
132. But whoever, hunting his own happiness, does not harm with the rod other beings who long for happiness too, will find happiness hereafter.
133. Speak harshly to no one, or those you wound will answer you in kind. Angry words are painful, and blow will fall on blow.
134. But if you can stay silent, like a gong that is cracked and gives no sound, then you have come close to Nirvana, for there is no more strife in you.
135. As a cowherd with his staff drives the cattle out to pasture, so do old age and death drive the life of every living thing.
136. Even while he is doing it, the fool does not see the harm in his evil deeds; but later he is scorched by what he has done, as if burned by fire.
137. Whoever takes up the rod against those who are unarmed and harmless, who wrongs the innocent, will quickly come to one of these ten states:
138. sharp pain, or disaster, or injury to the body, or grave illness, or loss of his mind;
139. or trouble from those in power, or a terrible accusation, or the loss of his family, or the ruin of all he owns;
140. or fire will burn his house to the ground. And when his body breaks apart, the fool is reborn in hell.

141. Not going naked, not matted hair, not filth, not fasting, not sleeping on the bare ground, not smearing the body with dust, not crouching motionless—none of these can cleanse a person who has not gone beyond his cravings.

142. But the one who is calm even though finely dressed, who is still, restrained, and self-controlled, who lives a pure life and has laid down the rod against every living thing—he is the true Brahmin, the true ascetic, the true monk.
143. Is there anywhere in the world a person so restrained by his own sense of shame that he gives no cause for blame, as a fine horse gives no cause for the whip?

144. Be like a fine horse that breaks into a run at the touch of the whip: be eager and alive. By faith, by virtue, by effort, by deep meditation, by clear judgment of the truth, by right knowledge and right conduct, with full awareness, you will leave this great suffering behind.
145. Farmers channel the water where they want it; arrow-makers straighten the shaft; carpenters shape the wood; and the good shape themselves.
146. What laughter, what joy, when the world is forever burning? Wrapped in darkness as you are, why do you not seek a light?
147. Look at this body, all dressed up — a mass of wounds, a thing of patched-together parts, sickly, full of cravings, with nothing in it that lasts.
148. This body is worn out, a nest of disease, ready to fall apart. This rotting heap breaks to pieces; life ends in death.
149. These white bones, scattered like gourds thrown away in autumn — what pleasure is there in looking at them?
150. The body is a fortress built of bones and plastered over with flesh and blood, and inside it live old age and death, pride and deceit.
151. Even the gleaming chariots of kings wear out, and the body too is wearing toward its end. But the virtue of the good never wears out — so the good pass it on, one to another.
152. The person who has learned little grows old like an ox: his body grows heavier, but his wisdom does not grow.

153, 154. Through many births I ran on, seeking and never finding the builder of this house — and painful is birth, again and again. House-builder, now you are seen! You shall not build this house again. Your rafters are all broken, your ridgepole shattered. My mind has reached the unmade, the unconditioned, Nirvana; I have come to the end of craving.
155. Those who have kept no discipline, and have gathered no treasure in their youth, waste away like old herons beside a lake that has no fish.
156. Those who have kept no discipline, and have gathered no treasure in their youth, lie like worn-out bows, sighing over the past.
157. If you hold yourself dear, then guard yourself well. Through at least one of the three watches of the night, let the wise stay awake and watchful.
158. First set yourself in what is right; only then teach others. The wise who do this bring no blame upon themselves.
159. Do for yourself what you would have others do; train yourself before you train anyone else, for the self is the hardest of all to master. Only the well-mastered are fit to master others.
160. You are your own master; who else could be? With yourself well mastered, you have found a master few ever find.
161. The evil you do is your own; it is born of you, bred by you, and it grinds the fool down as a diamond grinds the gem it was cut from.
162. The one whose wickedness runs deep drags himself down to the very ruin his enemy would wish for him, as a strangling vine drags down the tree it has wrapped.
163. Things that harm you, and that do you no good, are all too easy to do. What is good and brings you benefit is the hardest thing of all to do.

164. The fool who scorns the teaching of the worthy ones, the Noble Ones, the upright, and follows a false doctrine instead, bears fruit only to his own destruction, like the reed that dies the year it flowers.
165. By yourself the wrong is done; by yourself you are stained. By yourself the wrong is left undone; by yourself you are made pure. Purity and impurity are your own; no one can purify another.
166. However great another's good may be, do not neglect your own true good for it. Once you have seen clearly what your own good is, give yourself to it.
167. Do not follow the low way. Do not live in heedlessness. Do not take up false views. Do not be a friend of the world.
168. Rouse yourself! Do not be idle! Follow the path of virtue. The virtuous rest in peace, in this world and the next.
169. Follow the path of virtue, not the way of wrongdoing. The virtuous rest in peace, in this world and the next.
170. Look on the world as a bubble; look on it as a mirage. The King of Death never sees the one who sees the world this way.
171. Come, look at this glittering world, like a painted royal chariot. Fools sink into it, but the wise take no hold of it.
172. The one who was heedless before, and afterward grows heedful, lights up this world like the moon set free from a cloud.
173. The one whose evil deeds are covered over by good lights up this world like the moon set free from a cloud.
174. This world is blind; only a few here see clearly. Only a few reach heaven, like birds slipping free of the net.
175. Swans travel the path of the sun; the adept travel through the air by their own spiritual power. The wise are led out of this world once they have conquered Mara and all his army.
176. The one who breaks the single law of truth, who speaks lies and mocks the world to come, will stop at no evil.
177. The stingy never reach the world of the gods; only fools have no praise for giving. The wise rejoice in giving, and so find happiness in the world to come.
178. Better than sole rule over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of the first step into the stream.

179. The one whose conquest cannot be undone, into whose conquest no craving in this world can enter—by what track will you trace him, the Awakened One, whose knowing is endless, who leaves no trail at all?
180. The one whom no desire, with all its nets and poisons, can lead anywhere astray—by what track will you trace him, the Awakened One, whose knowing is endless, who leaves no trail at all?
181. Even the gods envy the wise—those who are awake and never heedless, who give themselves to meditation, who delight in the peace of letting the world go.
182. Hard it is to be born a human being; hard is the life of mortals; hard it is to hear the true teaching; and hardest of all, rare beyond rare, is the arising of a Buddha, an Awakened One.
183. Not to do any evil; to cultivate good; to purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of all the Buddhas, the Awakened Ones.
184. Patience and endurance are the highest austerity; "Nirvana is the highest," say the Buddhas. The one who strikes another is no true renouncer; the one who wounds another is no true seeker.

185. To speak no blame and do no harm; to live restrained under the rule of the teaching; to eat in moderation; to keep to a solitary bed and seat; and to give the mind to the highest things—this is the teaching of the Awakened.
186. There is no satisfying the craving for pleasure, not even with a downpour of gold. "Pleasures are sweet for a moment and end in pain"—the wise know this.
187. So the disciple who is fully awake takes no delight even in the pleasures of heaven; he delights only in the ending of all craving.
188. Driven by fear, people run for refuge to many places—to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees.
189. But that is not the safe refuge, that is not the highest refuge; taking refuge there, you are not freed from all suffering.
190. The one who takes refuge in the Buddha, in the Dhamma—the Law—and in the Sangha—the Order—and who sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:
191. that there is suffering; that suffering has a cause; that suffering can be brought to an end; and that there is the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the end of suffering—
192. that is the safe refuge, that is the highest refuge; taking that refuge, you are freed from all suffering.
193. A great one, a Buddha, is hard to find; he is not born just anywhere. But wherever such a sage is born, that people flourishes.
194. Happy is the arising of the Awakened; happy is the teaching of the true Law; happy is the harmony of the Order; happy is the practice of those who live in harmony.

195, 196. Whoever honors those worthy of honor—whether the Awakened Buddhas or their disciples—who have left every obstacle behind and crossed beyond all grief and longing; whoever honors such ones, set free and past all fear, his merit is beyond all measuring; no one can reckon how great it is.
197. Let us live happily, then, free of hatred among those who hate. Among people who hate, let us live free of hatred.
198. Let us live happily, then, in good health among the sick. Among people who are sick, let us live in good health.
199. Let us live happily, then, free of greed among the greedy. Among people who are greedy, let us live free of greed.
200. Let us live happily, then, owning nothing at all. We will feed on joy, like the bright gods of streaming light.
201. Victory breeds hatred, and the defeated lie down in pain. Letting go of both victory and defeat, the peaceful lie down happy.
202. There is no fire like craving, no losing throw like hatred, no suffering like the burden of body and mind, no happiness higher than peace.
203. Hunger is the worst of diseases; the things we are made of are the worst of burdens. See this as it truly is, and you see Nirvana, the highest happiness.
204. Health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth, a trusted friend the best of kin, and Nirvana the highest happiness.
205. Having tasted the sweetness of solitude and of peace, you are freed of fear and freed of wrong, drinking in the sweetness of the truth.
206. Good it is to see the Noble Ones; to live with them is always happiness. Keep clear of fools, and you will be happy indeed.
207. Whoever keeps company with fools grieves a long road; company with fools is painful, like company with an enemy, while company with the wise is a joy, like the welcome of kin.
208. So follow the good and the wise, the steadfast, the learned, the enduring, the faithful, the Noble — follow such a one, good and wise, as the moon follows the path of the stars.
209. Whoever gives himself to what does not matter, and not to meditation, who lets go of the real aim and grabs at pleasure instead, will one day envy the person who held to the path.
210. Do not bind yourself to the pleasant or to the unpleasant. Not to see what you love is pain, and to see what you hate is pain.
211. So hold nothing dear, for to lose what you hold dear is misery. Those who hold nothing dear and hate nothing have no chains to bind them.
212. From what is dear comes grief; from what is dear comes fear. To one who holds nothing dear there is no grief, so where would fear come from?
213. From affection comes grief; from affection comes fear. To one free of affection there is no grief, so where would fear come from?
214. From attachment comes grief; from attachment comes fear. To one free of attachment there is no grief, so where would fear come from?
215. From lust comes grief; from lust comes fear. To one free of lust there is no grief, so where would fear come from?
216. From craving comes grief; from craving comes fear. To one free of craving there is no grief, so where would fear come from?
217. The one who is perfect in virtue and in insight, who is just, who speaks the truth, and who does the work that is his own to do—him the world holds dear.

218. The one in whom a longing for the Ineffable, Nirvana, has awakened, whose mind is filled with it, and whose thoughts are no longer caught by the pleasures of the senses—that one is called a swimmer against the stream.
219. When a man long away from home returns safe from afar, his kinsmen, his friends, and those who love him welcome him back with joy.
220. In just this way, when one who has done good passes from this world to the next, his good deeds welcome him home—as kinsmen welcome a loved one come back at last.
221. Give up anger, let go of pride, break free of every fetter. No suffering can fall on the one who clings to neither name nor form, and who calls nothing his own.
222. The one who holds back rising anger as a driver reins in a runaway chariot—him I call a true charioteer. The rest merely hold the reins.
223. Overcome anger by calm, evil by good; overcome the miser by giving, the liar by truth.
224. Speak the truth, do not give way to anger, give when you are asked, even if you have little. By these three steps you draw near to the gods.
225. The sages who harm no one, who keep their bodies always under control, go to the unchanging place, Nirvana, and once they have gone there, they suffer no more.
226. For those who are always wakeful, who train themselves day and night, whose whole aim is Nirvana, every craving comes to an end.

227. This is an old saying, Atula, not something new: they blame the one who sits silent, they blame the one who talks a great deal, and they blame the one who speaks in moderation. There is no one in the world who is not blamed.
228. There never was, and never will be, and is not now, anyone who is only blamed or only praised.

229, 230. But the one whom the discerning praise day after day—flawless, wise, rich in understanding and in virtue—who would dare to blame, worthy as a coin of the purest river-gold? Even the gods praise such a one; even Brahman praises him.
231. Guard against the anger of the body; keep your body under control. Give up the wrongs of the body, and with your body do what is good.
232. Guard against the anger of speech; keep your speech under control. Give up the wrongs of speech, and with your speech do what is good.
233. Guard against the anger of the mind; keep your mind under control. Give up the wrongs of the mind, and with your mind do what is good.
234. The wise who control the body, who control speech, who control the mind—they are the ones who are truly well controlled.
235. You are now like a withered leaf; the messengers of death are already at hand. You stand at the threshold of departure, and you have packed no provisions for the road.
236. Make an island of yourself. Strive hard; be wise. Once you have blown away your impurities and are free of all stain, you will enter the heavenly realm of the Noble Ones.
237. Your life has run its course; you have come face to face with death. There is no resting place for you along the way, and you have packed no provisions for the road.
238. Make an island of yourself. Strive hard; be wise. Once you have blown away your impurities and are free of all stain, you will not enter again into birth and decay.
239. Let the wise blow away their own impurities, one by one, little by little, moment by moment, as a smith blows the dross from silver.
240. Just as rust, springing from the iron itself, eats away the very iron that bred it, so a transgressor's own deeds lead him down to ruin.
241. Scriptures decay when they go unrecited; houses decay when they go unrepaired; beauty decays through sloth; a watchman decays through carelessness.
242. Misconduct is the taint of a woman; stinginess is the taint of a giver. Tainted are all evil ways, in this world and the next.
243. But there is a taint worse than all these: ignorance is the greatest taint of all. Cast off that taint, monks, and become taintless.
244. Life is easy for the shameless one, brazen as a crow, a meddler, a slanderer, insolent and corrupt.
245. But life is hard for the modest one, who always seeks what is pure, who is detached, unassuming, clean, and clear-sighted.
246. Whoever destroys life, speaks falsehood, takes in this world what is not given, and goes to another man's wife;
247. and whoever gives himself to strong drink—that person, even here in this world, digs up his own roots.
248. Know this, friend: those who cannot hold themselves in check come to a bad end. Do not let greed and vice drag you into long suffering.
249. People give according to their faith, according to what pleases them. But whoever frets over the food and drink given to others will find no peace, by day or by night.
250. The one in whom that fretting is destroyed, torn out by the very root, finds peace by day and by night.
251. There is no fire like craving, no grip like hatred, no snare like delusion, no torrent like greed.
252. The faults of others are easy to see; our own are hard to see. We winnow the faults of our neighbors like chaff, but hide our own, as a cheat hides the losing throw from the gambler.
253. Whoever watches for the faults of others, forever taking offense, only feeds his own cravings; he comes no nearer to their end.
254. There is no path through the sky; outward acts do not make a holy man. People delight in what holds them back, but the Tathagatas, the Buddhas, are free of all such hindrance.
255. There is no path through the sky; outward acts do not make a holy man. Nothing made of conditions lasts, but the Buddhas are never shaken.
256. You are not just because you settle a case in haste. The wise weigh both sides, the right and the wrong, before they decide.
257. The one who judges others not by force but fairly, by what is right, who is guided by what is right and is discerning—that one is called just, established in dhamma.
258. You are not wise because you talk a great deal. The one who is patient, free of hatred, free of fear—that one is called wise.

259. You do not uphold the teaching because you talk a great deal. Even one who has learned only a little, but sees the truth in his own person, truly upholds the teaching—he is the one who never turns his back on it.
260. You are not an elder because your head is gray. To be ripe in years and no more than that is to be old in vain.

261. But the one in whom there is truth and virtue, who does no harm, who is restrained and master of himself, the wise one who has washed out every stain—he is the one who deserves to be called an elder.
262. No amount of fine talk, no beauty of face, will make a man worthy of respect if he is envious, grasping, and false.
263. But the one in whom all this is cut down, torn out by the very root—the one who has let go of hatred and grown wise—he is the one worthy of respect.
264. A shaved head does not make a man an ascetic if he has no discipline and speaks lies. How can anyone still gripped by craving and greed be an ascetic?
265. But the one who quiets every evil in himself, great or small, is an ascetic indeed, for he has stilled all evil.
266. You are not a monk simply because you beg your food from others. Whoever merely begs is not a monk; it is the one who takes up the whole teaching, and lives by it, who is.
267. The one who has risen above both good and evil, who lives a pure life and walks through the world with true understanding—he is the one truly called a monk.

268, 269. Silence does not make a sage of a man who is dull and ignorant. But the one who is wise, who holds up the scales and chooses the good and turns away from evil—he is a sage, and a sage for that very reason. The one who weighs both worlds is the one called a sage.
270. You are not noble if you do harm to living things. It is because he does no harm to any living thing that a man is called noble.

271, 272. Not by rules and vows alone, not by great learning, not by the depths of meditation, not by sleeping apart from others, do I touch the freedom and peace that no ordinary person knows. Monk, do not rest content until you have reached the end of craving.
273. Of all paths, the Eightfold Path is the best; of all truths, the Four Noble Truths; of all states, freedom from craving; and of all who have eyes, the one who truly sees—the Buddha.
274. This is the Way; there is no other that leads to the purifying of vision. Follow it, and you will bewilder Mara, the tempter.
275. Walk this Way and you will make an end of suffering. This is the Way I taught, once I had learned to draw out the arrow of craving.
276. You yourself must make the effort. The Buddhas only point the way. Those who take up the path and walk it, deep in meditation, are freed from the bonds of Mara.
277. "All conditioned things are impermanent" (sabbe sankhara anicca)—when you see this with wisdom, you turn away from suffering. This is the path to purity.
278. "All conditioned things are suffering" (sabbe sankhara dukkha)—when you see this with wisdom, you turn away from suffering. This is the path to purity.
279. "All things are without a self" (sabbe dhamma anatta)—when you see this with wisdom, you turn away from suffering. This is the path to purity.
280. The one who will not rouse himself when it is time to rise, who is young and strong but full of sloth, weak in will and weak in thought, that lazy and idle man never finds the way to wisdom.
281. Guard your speech, hold your mind in check, and do no wrong with your body. Keep these three roads of action clean, and you will win the way the wise have taught.
282. From effort wisdom grows; without effort it withers away. Knowing this double path—the one that gains and the one that loses—set yourself so that wisdom grows.
283. Cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree—for out of that forest comes fear. Clear away the forest and the undergrowth, monks, and you will be free.
284. As long as the least desire of a man for a woman is not cut away, his mind is tied down, like a suckling calf to its mother.
285. Cut out the love of self, as you would pluck an autumn lotus with your hand. Tend the road of peace—the Nirvana the Buddha has shown.
286. "Here I will live through the rains, and here through winter and summer"—so the fool plans, never thinking of his death.
287. But death comes and sweeps that man away—proud of his children and his herds, his mind on other things—as a flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
288. Sons are no help then, nor a father, nor any of your kin; once death has seized you, there is no help in family.
289. Knowing this, the wise and disciplined should clear the road at once—the road that leads to Nirvana.
290. If by giving up a lesser happiness one may gain a greater, let the wise give up the lesser and look to the greater.
291. Whoever seeks his own happiness by causing pain to others is caught in the bonds of hatred, and from hatred he is never freed.
292. What ought to be done is left undone, and what ought not to be done is done; in those who are unruly and heedless the taints keep on growing.

293. But in those who are always mindful of the body, who do not do what ought not to be done and steadily do what ought to be done, the taints, in such mindful and clear-seeing people, come to an end.
294. Having killed mother and father and two warrior kings, and having destroyed a kingdom along with its treasurer, the true Brahmin goes on his way unharmed.
295. Having killed mother and father and two learned kings, and having destroyed a kingdom along with its tiger, the true Brahmin goes on his way unharmed.
296. The followers of Gotama are always wide awake; day and night their thoughts are set on the Buddha.
297. The followers of Gotama are always wide awake; day and night their thoughts are set on the teaching.
298. The followers of Gotama are always wide awake; day and night their thoughts are set on the community.
299. The followers of Gotama are always wide awake; day and night their thoughts are set on the body.
300. The followers of Gotama are always wide awake; day and night their minds delight in doing no harm.
301. The followers of Gotama are always wide awake; day and night their minds delight in meditation.

302. Hard it is to leave the world; hard it is to enjoy the world. Hard is life in the monastery, and painful is life in a house; painful it is to live among those who are not your equals. And painful it is to keep wandering on through the round of birth and death—so do not be a wanderer who is hounded by that pain.
303. The one who has faith and virtue, who has a good name and means of his own, is honored wherever he goes.
304. The good are seen from far off, like the snowy peaks of the Himalayas; the bad pass unseen, like arrows shot in the night.
305. Sitting alone, sleeping alone, walking alone, never weary, taming himself alone—he will find his joy at the edge of the forest.

306. Whoever says what is not so goes to hell, and so does the one who, having done a thing, says, "I did not do it." After death both are alike—they are people who carry their wrongdoing into the next world.
307. Many a man whose shoulders are wrapped in the yellow robe is undisciplined and out of control; by their own wrongdoing such wrongdoers go to hell.
308. Better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, blazing like fire, than to live on the alms of the land while being immoral and undisciplined.
309. Four things come to the reckless man who goes after his neighbor's wife: he earns disgrace, his sleep is broken, third comes punishment, and last comes hell.

310. There is disgrace, and the road that leads downward, and only the brief pleasure of one frightened soul in the arms of another, and the king's heavy punishment. So let no man set his heart on his neighbor's wife.
311. Just as a blade of kusa grass, wrongly grasped, cuts the very hand that holds it, so the monk's life, wrongly lived, drags a man down to hell.
312. Anything done half-heartedly, a vow once broken, a discipline kept only grudgingly—none of it bears much fruit.
313. If a thing is worth doing, do it; throw yourself into it. A monk who wanders through his practice half-asleep only stirs up more of the dust of craving.
314. A wrong deed is better left undone, for afterward it brings regret; a right deed is better done, for having done it, you never look back with regret.
315. Like a frontier fort guarded inside and out, so guard yourself. Do not let a single moment slip past, for those who let the right moment pass suffer for it when they come to hell.
316. Those who are ashamed of what is no shame, and feel no shame at what truly should shame them—taking up wrong views, such people go down the wrong road.
317. Those who are afraid of what is no danger, and unafraid of what is truly dangerous—taking up wrong views, such people go down the wrong road.
318. Those who see fault where there is none, and see no fault where the fault is real—taking up wrong views, such people go down the wrong road.
319. But those who see fault as fault, and what is faultless as faultless—holding to right views, such people go down the right road.
320. I will bear abuse in silence, as the elephant in battle bears the arrow shot from the bow; for many people are ill-natured.
321. They lead a tamed elephant into battle; the king mounts a tamed elephant. The one who is tamed, who bears abuse in silence, is the best among people.
322. Good are tamed mules, and thoroughbred horses of Sindh, and great tusked elephants; but better than any of them is the one who has tamed himself.
323. For on none of these animals can you reach the untrodden country, Nirvana. Only the one who has tamed himself goes there—tamed, riding his own well-tamed self.
324. The elephant called Dhanapalaka, his temples streaming in must and hard to hold, will not eat a mouthful once he is tied up: the elephant is longing for the elephant-grove.
325. The man who is slack and overeats, who is drowsy and rolls about like a great hog fattened on slop, that fool is born again and again.
326. In the past this mind of mine wandered wherever it wished, wherever it liked, wherever it pleased. Now I will hold it firmly in check, as the trainer with his hook holds in a raging elephant.
327. Take heed; guard your own mind. Pull yourself out of the wrong path, as an elephant pulls itself out of the mud.
328. If you find a wise companion to walk with you, one who is prudent and lives well, then walk with them, glad and mindful, overcoming every danger.

329. If you find no wise companion to walk with you, none who is prudent and lives well, then walk alone—like a king who has left behind the kingdom he had won, like a Matanga elephant roaming the forest.
330. It is better to walk alone; there is no companionship with a fool. Walk alone and do no wrong, wanting little, like a Matanga elephant in the forest.
331. Friends are a joy when the need for them arises. Contentment is a joy, whatever brings it. A good deed done is a joy at the hour of death. And the laying down of all sorrow is a joy.
332. To be a good mother in this world is a joy, and to be a good father is a joy; to live as one who has gone forth is a joy, and to live as a holy one is a joy.
333. A joy is virtue that lasts into old age; a joy is faith firmly rooted; a joy is the winning of wisdom; and a joy is to do no evil.
334. The craving of a heedless person grows like a creeping vine. He leaps from one life to the next, like a monkey swinging through the forest after fruit.
335. Whomever this fierce, poisonous craving overcomes in this world, his sorrows grow thick and fast, like wild grass after rain.
336. But whoever masters this fierce craving, so hard to overcome, finds his sorrows fall away from him, like water-drops sliding off a lotus leaf.

337. So here is the good word I give to all of you gathered here: dig up craving by the root, as one who wants the fragrant root digs up the grass above it—so that Mara, the tempter, may not break you again and again, as a flood breaks the reeds.
338. As a tree that has been cut down will grow again if its root is sound and deep, so suffering returns again and again until you dig out the very root of craving.
339. The man whose thirty-six streams of craving run strong toward pleasure is swept away: the flood of his own passionate longings carries him off.
340. These streams run everywhere; the vine of craving keeps springing up. When you see it sprouting, cut it at the root with wisdom.
341. People delight in pleasures, lavish and sweet. Sunk in their longing, chasing their pleasures, they go through birth and decay again and again.
342. Driven on by craving, people run round and round like a snared hare. Caught in fetters and bonds, they suffer, again and again, for a long time.
343. Driven on by craving, people run round and round like a snared hare. So let the seeker drive out craving, by working toward freedom from craving for himself.
344. Look at the man who has cut his way out of the thicket of craving, only to run straight back into it—who, set free, runs back into bondage of his own accord.
345. The wise do not call the strongest chain the one made of iron, or wood, or rope. Far stronger is the pull of jewels and rings, of children and wife—
346. that is the chain the wise call strong: it drags you down, it gives a little but will not let go. Yet even this they cut, and go forth, wanting nothing, leaving every pleasure behind.

347. Those enslaved by their passions are swept along the stream of desire, as a spider runs down the web it spun itself. This too the wise cut through, and go forth, wanting nothing, leaving every sorrow behind.
348. Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the present, and cross to the far shore of existence. With your mind set free on every side, you will come no more to birth and decay.
349. If a man is tossed about by doubt, burning with desire, fixed only on what delights him, his craving grows and grows, and the chain he forges grows only stronger.
350. But if a man delights in stilling his doubts, ever watchful, dwelling on what is not pleasant to the craving mind, he will surely make an end—he will cut clean through the chain of Mara.
351. The one who has reached the goal, who is fearless, free of craving and free of fault, has broken off every thorn of life. This is his last body.

352. The one free of craving and free of clinging, who is skilled in language and its meanings, who knows how words are formed and ordered—he wears his last body. He is called the great sage, the great person.

353. "I have conquered all and I know all. In every state of life I am untouched. I have let go of everything, and through the end of craving I am free. Knowing this for myself, whom should I call my teacher?"
354. The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes; the delight in the Dhamma surpasses all delights; the end of craving conquers all sorrow.
355. Wealth destroys the fool who does not look for the far shore. Through his thirst for wealth the fool destroys himself, as if he were his own enemy.
356. Weeds ruin a field; craving ruins those who give in to it. So a gift to those who are free of craving bears great fruit.
357. Weeds ruin a field; hatred ruins those who give in to it. So a gift to those who are free of hatred bears great fruit.
358. Weeds ruin a field; delusion ruins those who give in to it. So a gift to those who are free of delusion bears great fruit.
359. Weeds ruin a field; longing ruins those who give in to it. So a gift to those who are free of longing bears great fruit.
360. Restraint of the eye is good; good is restraint of the ear; good is restraint of the nose; good is restraint of the tongue.
361. Restraint of the body is good; good is restraint of speech; good is restraint of the mind; good is restraint in all things. The monk who is restrained in all things is freed from all suffering.

362. The one who controls his hands, who controls his feet, who controls his speech, who is master of himself; who takes his delight inwardly, who is composed, who is content alone — him they call a monk.
363. Sweet is the speech of the monk who masters his tongue, who speaks with wisdom and without pride, who makes plain the meaning and the teaching.
364. The monk who dwells in the teaching, who delights in the teaching, who meditates on the teaching, who keeps the teaching in mind, will never fall away from the true teaching.
365. Let him not despise what he himself has received, nor go about envying what others receive. The monk who envies others never comes to stillness of mind.
366. Though a monk receive but little, if he does not despise what he has received, even the gods will praise him — so long as his life is pure and he is not slack.
367. The one who never takes name and form to be himself, and does not grieve over what has passed away — he indeed is called a monk.
368. The monk who lives in loving-kindness, who has faith in the teaching of the Buddha, will reach the place of peace — Nirvana — where all that is conditioned is stilled, and there find happiness.
369. Empty this boat, O monk! Once emptied, it will move swiftly. Cut off craving and hatred, and you will come to Nirvana.
370. Cut off five, let go of five, and cultivate five more. The monk who has risen above the five attachments is called one who has crossed the flood.

371. Meditate, O monk, and do not be careless. Do not let your mind whirl after the pleasures of the senses. Be careless, and you may have to swallow the iron ball in hell, and cry out as you burn, "This is suffering!"
372. There is no meditation for one without wisdom, and no wisdom for one who does not meditate. The one in whom both meditation and wisdom are found stands close upon Nirvana.
373. The monk who has gone into an empty house, whose mind is at peace, who sees the teaching clearly, knows a joy that is more than human.
374. As soon as he grasps how the elements of body and mind rise and pass away, he finds the happiness and gladness that belong to those who know the deathless.
375. And here is where the wise monk begins: guarding the senses, contentment, restraint within the rule of the teaching. Let him keep noble friends whose lives are pure and who are not slack.
376. Let him be generous and warm-hearted, faultless in how he conducts himself; then, filled with gladness, he will make an end of suffering.
377. As the jasmine sheds its withered flowers, so, O monks, shed craving and hatred.
378. The monk whose body is stilled, whose speech is stilled, whose mind is stilled, who is composed, who has spat out the lures of the world — he is rightly called one who is at peace.
379. Rouse yourself by yourself; examine yourself by yourself. Guarding yourself and keeping watch, O monk, you will live in happiness.
380. For you are your own master, you are your own refuge. So hold yourself in check, as a horse-dealer reins in a fine horse.
381. The monk who is full of gladness, who has faith in the teaching of the Buddha, will reach the place of peace — Nirvana — where all that is conditioned is stilled, and there find happiness.
382. The monk who, though still young, gives himself to the teaching of the Buddha lights up this whole world, as the moon does when it breaks free of the clouds.
383. Cut off the stream of craving, Brahmin, and drive out your desires. Once you have understood the destruction of all that is made, you will know the Uncreated, Nirvana.
384. When the Brahmin has crossed to the far shore of both teachings—restraint and meditation—then for him who has reached this knowledge every bond falls away.
385. The one for whom there is no near shore, no far shore, nor any shore between, who is free of fear and free of every chain—him I call a true Brahmin.
386. The one who sits in meditation, free of dust, his work done, his passions gone, who has reached the highest goal—him I call a true Brahmin.

387. The sun is bright by day, the moon shines by night, the warrior is bright in his armor, the Brahmin is bright in his meditation; but the Buddha, the Awakened One, shines with splendor both day and night.

388. Because he has cast out evil, he is called a Brahmin; because he lives in peace, he is called a Samana, an ascetic; because he has driven out his own impurities, he is called Pabbajita, one gone forth.
389. No one should strike a Brahmin; and a Brahmin who is struck should not strike back in anger. Shame on the one who strikes a Brahmin, but greater shame on the Brahmin who strikes back.
390. It is no small good for a Brahmin to hold his mind back from the things it loves. The more the wish to harm dies away, the more his suffering comes to rest.
391. The one who does no wrong with body, speech, or mind, who keeps himself in check on all three—him I call a true Brahmin.
392. From whomever you have learned the teaching of the Awakened One, honor that person with all your heart, as a Brahmin honors the sacred fire.
393. Not by matted hair, not by lineage, not by birth does one become a Brahmin. The one in whom there is truth and righteousness—he is the pure one, he is the Brahmin.
394. What good is your matted hair, you fool? What good your cloak of goatskins? Outside you keep yourself clean, but inside you are a tangle of craving.
395. The one who wears cast-off rags, worn thin to the bone, who lives alone in the forest and meditates—him I call a true Brahmin.

396. I do not call anyone a Brahmin merely because of the mother who bore him or the family he came from. If he is full of pride and clings to his possessions, he is only a man who says "sir" to himself. But the one who owns nothing and clings to nothing—him I call a true Brahmin.
397. The one who has cut every fetter, who never trembles, who is beyond all ties and free of every chain—him I call a true Brahmin.
398. The one who has cut the strap and the rein, the rope and the harness with it, who has thrown off the bar across the gate and is awake—him I call a true Brahmin.
399. The one who endures abuse, blows, and prison without anger, though he has done no wrong, whose strength is his patience and whose army is his endurance—him I call a true Brahmin.
400. The one who is free of anger, faithful to his duty, virtuous, without craving, mastered, wearing this body for the last time—him I call a true Brahmin.
401. The one who does not cling to pleasures any more than water clings to a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed clings to the point of a needle—him I call a true Brahmin.
402. The one who knows, here and now, the end of his own suffering, who has laid down his burden and is free of every chain—him I call a true Brahmin.
403. The one whose wisdom is deep, who knows the way from the wrong way, and who has reached the highest goal—him I call a true Brahmin.
404. The one who keeps apart from householders and homeless alike, who wanders without a home and wants almost nothing—him I call a true Brahmin.
405. The one who has laid down all violence toward every living thing, weak or strong, who neither kills nor causes others to kill—him I call a true Brahmin.
406. The one who stays gentle among the hostile, peaceful among the violent, and free of clinging among those who cling—him I call a true Brahmin.
407. The one from whom anger and hatred, pride and contempt have fallen away, like a mustard seed from the point of a needle—him I call a true Brahmin.
408. The one who speaks the truth, words that teach and never wound, words that give offense to no one—him I call a true Brahmin.
409. The one who takes nothing in this world that is not given to him, be it long or short, small or large, fair or foul—him I call a true Brahmin.
410. The one who has no longing for this world or the next, who is free of all desire and every chain—him I call a true Brahmin.
411. The one who has nothing left to cling to, who has understood and is free of all doubt, with no more "how?" and "why?", who has plunged into the deathless—him I call a true Brahmin.
412. The one who has risen above both good and evil here, beyond the pull of either, untouched by sorrow, passion, and stain—him I call a true Brahmin.
413. The one who is bright as the moon, clear and still, untroubled, in whom all craving for becoming has burned out—him I call a true Brahmin.

414. The one who has crossed this swamp, this rough and trackless road of wandering and delusion, and reached the far shore—a meditator, free of craving and of doubt, clinging to nothing, perfectly at peace—him I call a true Brahmin.
415. The one who has left every desire behind, who wanders homeless in this world, in whom all hunger for pleasure has burned out—him I call a true Brahmin.
416. The one who has left every craving behind, who wanders homeless in this world, in whom all greed has burned out—him I call a true Brahmin.
417. The one who has thrown off every human bond and risen beyond every heavenly bond, free of all bonds whatever—him I call a true Brahmin.
418. The one who has left behind what gives pleasure and what gives pain, grown cool, with nothing left to seed another birth—the hero who has conquered every world—him I call a true Brahmin.
419. The one who knows how beings pass away and rise again, everywhere, who clings to nothing, who has gone the happy way and is awake—him I call a true Brahmin.
420. The one whose path the gods cannot trace, nor the spirits, nor men, in whom every passion has burned out, an Arhat, the worthy one—him I call a true Brahmin.
421. The one who calls nothing his own—not what is past, not what is to come, not what is now—who owns nothing and grasps at nothing—him I call a true Brahmin.
422. The bull among men, the noble one, the hero, the great sage, the conqueror, the one beyond all desire, washed clean, awake—him I call a true Brahmin.
423. The one who knows his former lives, who sees the heavens and the hells, who has come to the end of all births, a sage perfected in knowledge, whose work is wholly done—him I call a true Brahmin.
